    Where N and M are dimensions of the grid and L is the length of the word. For each cell, we check 8 directions.

  • Space Complexity: O(K)
    Where K is the number of starting positions found.

✅ Notes

  • This is a classic implementation problem with directional search.
  • Efficient handling of bounds and direction logic is key.
  • Avoid duplicates in output when the word appears in multiple directions from the same starting cell.

Problem Statement:243¶

Smallest Greater Elements in Whole Array Given an array A of length N. For each element in the array, find the smallest greater element that exists anywhere else in the array.

  • If such an element does not exist, place -10000000 at that index in the result.

📥 Input

  • An integer array arr[] of size n.

📤 Output

  • An integer array of size n where each element is the smallest greater element in the array than the current element.
  • If no such element exists, the value should be -10000000.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
  • -10^9 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10^9

Goal:
For each element in the array, find the smallest greater element anywhere else in the array; if none exists, output -10000000.

🧠 Approach

  1. Copy and Sort the Array:

    • Sort a copy of the input array to get all possible greater elements in order.

  2. Binary Search for Each Element:

    • For each element, find the next smallest greater element using binary search on the sorted array.

  3. Return the Result:

    • If a greater element is found, store it in the result.
    • Else, store -10000000.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Copy input array and sort it
  • For each element in original array:
    • Binary search for smallest element greater than current element in sorted array
    • If found, record it in result
    • Else record -10000000
  • Return result array
  • End

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function greaterElement(arr):
sortedArr = sorted copy of arr
result = array of length n

for i in 0 to n-1:
    val = arr[i]
    nextGreater = binarySearchNextGreater(sortedArr, val)
    if nextGreater exists:
        result[i] = nextGreater
    else:
        result[i] = -10000000

return result

function binarySearchNextGreater(sortedArr, val):
left = 0
right = length(sortedArr) - 1
res = -10000000

while left <= right:
    mid = (left + right) // 2
    if sortedArr[mid] > val:
        res = sortedArr[mid]
        right = mid - 1
    else:
        left = mid + 1

return res

💻 Java Code

class Complete {
    
    private static int findNextGreater(int[] sortedArr, int val) {
        int left = 0, right = sortedArr.length - 1;
        int res = -10000000;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (sortedArr[mid] > val) {
                res = sortedArr[mid];
                right = mid - 1;
            } else {
                left = mid + 1;
            }
        }

        return res;
    }

    public static int[] greaterElement(int arr[], int n) {
        int[] result = new int[n];
        int[] sorted = Arrays.copyOf(arr, n);
        Arrays.sort(sorted);

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            result[i] = findNextGreater(sorted, arr[i]);
        }

        return result;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n log n) (due to sorting + binary search for each element)
  • Space Complexity: O(n) (for result and sorted array)

✅ Notes

  • Since the array may contain duplicates, the next greater element can be any occurrence that is strictly greater than the current element, not necessarily at a higher index.
  • Using a sorted copy and binary search efficiently finds the smallest greater element in O(log n) time for each element.
  • The sentinel value -10000000 is used to indicate the absence of a greater element.
  • Sorting takes O(n log n), and each binary search is O(log n), resulting in an overall O(n log n) time complexity.
  • Space is O(n) due to storing the sorted array and the output array.

Problem Statement: 244¶

Validate an IP Address
You are given a string s in the form of an IPv4 address. Your task is to validate the IPv4 address. If it is valid, return true; otherwise, return false.

An IPv4 address must be of the format x1.x2.x3.x4 where each x is a number between 0 and 255, and there must be no leading zeros (except for single 0). Each segment must only contain digits, and the address must contain exactly three dots.

📥 Input

  • A string ipStr representing an IPv4 address.

📤 Output

  • Return true if the input string is a valid IPv4 address.
  • Otherwise, return false.

Example
Input:
s = "192.168.1.1"
Output:
true

Constraints:

  • The input string length can vary but must adhere to IPv4 formatting rules.
  • Only digits and dots are allowed in the input string.

Goal:
To verify if the given string is a valid IPv4 address based on format and numeric rules.

🧠 Approach

  1. Check for 3 Dots:

    • An IPv4 address must have exactly 3 dots to form 4 parts.

  2. Tokenize by Dot (.)

    • Split the string using dot (.) as the delimiter.

  3. Validate Each Part:

    • Each part must be numeric.
    • No part should have leading zeros (e.g., 01, 001 are invalid).
    • Each part should be between 0 and 255.

  4. Return True/False:

    • If all parts are valid and count of parts is 4, return true.
    • Otherwise, return false.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Check if string has exactly 3 dots
  • Split the string by '.' into 4 parts
  • For each part:
    • Check if numeric and length ≤ 3
    • Check no leading zeros unless single '0'
    • Check integer value in range 0-255
  • If all checks pass, return true
  • Else, return false

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function isValidIP(ipStr):
if ipStr is null or does not contain exactly 3 dots:
return false
parts = split ipStr by '.'
if length(parts) != 4:
return false
for each part in parts:
if not isValidPart(part):
return false
return true

function isValidPart(part):
if length(part) == 0 or length(part) > 3:
return false
if part contains non-digit characters:
return false
if part has leading zero and length > 1:
return false
val = integer value of part
if val < 0 or val > 255:
return false
return true

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    private static boolean isValidPart(String s) {
        int n = s.length();

        if (n > 3)
            return false;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            if (!(s.charAt(i) >= '0' && s.charAt(i) <= '9'))
                return false;

        if (s.indexOf('0') == 0 && n > 1)
            return false;

        try {
            int x = Integer.parseInt(s);
            return (x >= 0 && x <= 255);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    public boolean isValid(String ipStr) {
        if (ipStr == null)
            return false;

        int dots = 0;
        int len = ipStr.length();
        int count = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
            if (ipStr.charAt(i) == '.')
                count++;
        if (count != 3)
            return false;

        StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer(ipStr, ".");

        while (st.hasMoreTokens()) {
            String part = st.nextToken();
            if (isValidPart(part)) {
                if (st.hasMoreTokens())
                    dots++;
            } else {
                return false;
            }
        }

        return dots == 3;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the length of the string.
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Notes:

  • Leading zeros are not allowed except for the single digit zero.
  • The string must have exactly 3 dots dividing it into 4 parts.
  • The use of StringTokenizer or split helps separate the string efficiently.
  • This method does not allow extra characters or spaces in the input string.

Problem Statement: 245¶

Maximum Sub Array
Given an array of integers, find the contiguous subarray with the maximum sum that contains only non-negative numbers.

If there are multiple subarrays with the same maximum sum, return the one with the smallest starting index.

A subarray is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of elements within an array.

📥 Input

  • An integer array arr[] of size n.

📤 Output

  • An ArrayList<Integer> representing the subarray with the maximum sum consisting only of non-negative numbers.
  • If there is no such subarray (i.e., all elements are negative), return [-1].

Example
Input:
arr = [1, 2, 5, -7, 2, 3]
Output:
[1, 2, 5]
Explanation:
The subarray [1, 2, 5] has the maximum sum of 8 and contains only non-negative numbers.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= n <= 10^6
  • -10^9 <= arr[i] <= 10^9

Goal:
To find the contiguous subarray with the maximum sum consisting only of non-negative numbers, and in case of ties, choose the earliest starting subarray.

🧠 Approach

  1. Iterate Over Array:

    • Track the current subarray sum and starting index when you encounter non-negative numbers.

  2. Track Best Subarray:

    • If a new non-negative subarray has a higher sum or same sum but longer length, update the best range.

  3. Reset on Negative:

    • If a negative number is encountered, reset the current sum.

  4. Return Result:

    • If no valid subarray was found, return [-1].
    • Otherwise, return the subarray from bestStart to bestEnd.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Initialize maxSum, currSum, start indices
  • Iterate through the array:
    • If element is non-negative, add to currSum
    • If currSum > maxSum or (currSum == maxSum and current length longer), update best subarray indices
    • If element is negative, reset currSum and start
  • Return the best subarray or [-1] if none found

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function maxNonNegativeSubarray(arr):
maxSum = -1
currSum = 0
start = 0
bestStart = -1
bestEnd = -1

for i in range(len(arr)):
    if arr[i] >= 0:
        currSum += arr[i]
        if currSum == arr[i]:
            start = i
        if currSum > maxSum or (currSum == maxSum and (i - start) > (bestEnd - bestStart)):
            maxSum = currSum
            bestStart = start
            bestEnd = i
    else:
        currSum = 0

if bestStart == -1:
    return [-1]
else:
    return arr[bestStart : bestEnd + 1]

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public ArrayList<Integer> findSubarray(int arr[]) {
        ArrayList<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        int n = arr.length;

        int maxSum = -1;
        int currSum = 0;
        int start = 0;
        int bestStart = -1, bestEnd = -1;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (arr[i] >= 0) {
                currSum += arr[i];

                if (currSum == arr[i]) {
                    start = i;
                }

                if (currSum > maxSum || 
                    (currSum == maxSum && (i - start > bestEnd - bestStart))) {
                    maxSum = currSum;
                    bestStart = start;
                    bestEnd = i;
                }
            } else {
                currSum = 0;
            }
        }

        if (bestStart == -1) {
            result.add(-1);
            return result;
        }

        for (int i = bestStart; i <= bestEnd; i++) {
            result.add(arr[i]);
        }

        return result;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n) — Single pass over the array.
  • Space Complexity: O(k) — Output list for the resulting subarray of length k.

Notes:

  • The condition currSum == arr[i] helps track the start of a new non-negative subarray after reset.
  • Tie-breaker by length ensures the earliest longest subarray with max sum is chosen.
  • If all elements are negative, return [-1].

Problem Statement: 246¶

Reverse Words
Given a string s, reverse the order of words in the string without reversing the individual words themselves.
Words are separated by spaces.

📥 Input

  • A single string s which may contain:
    • Leading or trailing spaces
    • Multiple spaces between words

📤 Output

  • A string where the words are in reverse order
  • Only a single space separates the words
  • No leading or trailing spaces in the result

Example
Input:
" the sky is blue "
Output:
"blue is sky the"
Explanation:
The words are reversed in order and extra spaces removed.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= s.length <= 10^4
  • s consists of English letters and spaces.

Goal:
Reverse the order of words while handling multiple and trailing spaces properly.

🧠 Approach

  1. Trim the String:

    • Remove leading and trailing spaces using trim().

  2. Split by Whitespace:

    • Use regular expression \\s+ to split by one or more spaces.

  3. Reverse the Words Array:

    • Use two pointers to reverse the words in place.

  4. Join the Array into a String:

    • Use String.join(" ", array) to reconstruct the string with single spaces.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Trim input string
  • Split string by one or more spaces
  • Reverse the array of words
  • Join the reversed words with a single space
  • Return the resulting string

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function reverseWords(s):
s = trim(s)
words = split s by regex \s+
reverse words array
return join words with " "

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    // Function to reverse words in a given string
    public String reverseWords(String s) {
        // Trim leading and trailing spaces
        s = s.trim();

        // Split the string by one or more spaces
        String[] words = s.split("\\s+");

        // Reverse the array of words
        int left = 0, right = words.length - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            String temp = words[left];
            words[left] = words[right];
            words[right] = temp;
            left++;
            right--;
        }

        // Join words with a single space
        return String.join(" ", words);
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n) — One pass for splitting, one for reversing, and one for joining.
  • Space Complexity: O(n) — For storing words and the resulting string.

Notes:

  • Using regex \\s+ ensures multiple spaces are treated as a single delimiter.
  • Trimming removes unwanted leading/trailing spaces before processing.
  • Reversing is done in-place to optimize space.

Problem Statement: 247¶

Wildcard Pattern Matching
Given two strings pat and txt which may be of different sizes, determine if the wildcard pattern pat matches the entire string txt.

  • The pattern string pat can include special wildcard characters:
    • ? matches any single character
    • * matches any sequence of characters (including the empty sequence)

The match must cover the entire txt, not just a part of it.

📥 Input

  • A string pat — the wildcard pattern
  • A string txt — the text to be matched

📤 Output

  • Return true if the pattern matches the text, otherwise false

Example
Input:

pat = "a\*b?c"
txt = "axxbbc"

Output:

true

Explanation:
* matches "xx", ? matches "b", rest characters match exactly.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= pat.length, txt.length <= 10^4
  • pat and txt consist of lowercase English letters and wildcard characters.

Goal:
Determine if the pattern pat matches the entire text txt using wildcards ? and *.

🧠 Approach

  1. Dynamic Programming (DP) Table:

    • Use a 2D DP table dp[i][j] where:
      • dp[i][j] is true if the first i characters of txt match the first j characters of pat.

  2. Initialization:

    • dp[0][0] = true (empty pattern matches empty text)
    • Handle leading * in pattern by propagating true in the first row.

  3. Transition:

    • If characters match or pattern has ?: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]
    • If pattern has *:
      dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-1] (matches empty)
      || dp[i-1][j] (matches one or more characters)

  4. Result:

    • Final result will be in dp[n][m]

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Initialize DP table
  • Handle empty pattern and empty text cases
  • Iterate over each character of txt and pat
  • Update DP based on match, '?' or '*' rules
  • Return dp[n][m]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

initialize dp array of size (n+1) x (m+1)
dp\[0]\[0] = true
for j from 1 to m:
if pat\[j-1] == '*':
dp\[0]\[j] = dp\[0]\[j-1]
for i from 1 to n:
for j from 1 to m:
if pat\[j-1] == txt\[i-1] or pat\[j-1] == '?':
dp\[i]\[j] = dp\[i-1]\[j-1]
else if pat\[j-1] == '*':
dp\[i]\[j] = dp\[i]\[j-1] or dp\[i-1]\[j]
return dp\[n]\[m]

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public boolean wildCard(String txt, String pat) {
        int n = txt.length();
        int m = pat.length();

        boolean[][] dp = new boolean[n + 1][m + 1];
        dp[0][0] = true;

        for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++)
            if (pat.charAt(j - 1) == '*')
                dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 1];

        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++) {
                if (pat.charAt(j - 1) == txt.charAt(i - 1) || pat.charAt(j - 1) == '?') {
                    dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1];
                } else if (pat.charAt(j - 1) == '*') {
                    dp[i][j] = dp[i][j - 1] || dp[i - 1][j];
                }
            }
        }

        return dp[n][m];
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n * m)
  • Space Complexity: O(n * m)
    Where n = txt.length() and m = pat.length()

Notes:

  • DP approach avoids exponential recursion due to overlapping subproblems.
  • * can match zero or more characters, handled by dp[i][j-1] and dp[i-1][j].
  • ? matches exactly one character.
  • Efficient solution compared to naive backtracking.

Problem Statement: 248¶

0 - 1 Knapsack Problem
You are given n items, each with a specific weight and value, and a knapsack with capacity W. Your task is to select items to put into the knapsack so that:

  • The total weight of selected items does not exceed W.
  • The total value of selected items is maximized.

Note:

  • You can either include an item fully or exclude it — no partial inclusion.
  • Each item is available only once.

📥 Input

  • An integer W — maximum capacity of the knapsack
  • An integer array val[] — values of the items
  • An integer array wt[] — weights of the items

📤 Output

  • Return the maximum value that can be put into the knapsack

Example
Input:

W = 50
val = \[60, 100, 120]
wt = \[10, 20, 30]

Output:

220

Explanation:
Choose items with weights 20 and 30 for max value 100 + 120 = 220.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= n <= 1000
  • 1 <= W <= 10^5
  • 1 <= val[i], wt[i] <= 10^5

Goal:
Maximize total value in knapsack without exceeding capacity, selecting each item at most once.

🧠 Approach

  1. Recursive DP with Memoization:

    • Use a helper function knapsackRec(W, val, wt, n, memo) where:
      • W is remaining capacity
      • n is the number of items to consider
      • memo[n][W] stores the result to avoid recomputation

  2. Recursive Choices:

    • If weight of current item <= W, you have two options:
      • Include it: add its value and recurse with reduced capacity
      • Exclude it: move to the next item
    • Take the maximum of these two choices

  3. Memoization Table:

    • Use a 2D array memo[n+1][W+1] initialized to -1 to store results

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Initialize memoization table
  • For each item, decide to pick or not pick
  • Update memo with max values
  • Return max value for full capacity and all items

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function knapsackRec(W, val, wt, n, memo):
if n == 0 or W == 0:
return 0
if memo\[n]\[W] != -1:
return memo\[n]\[W]

if wt[n-1] <= W:
    pick = val[n-1] + knapsackRec(W - wt[n-1], val, wt, n-1, memo)
else:
    pick = 0

notPick = knapsackRec(W, val, wt, n-1, memo)
memo[n][W] = max(pick, notPick)
return memo[n][W]

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    static int knapsackRec(int W, int[] val, int[] wt, int n, int[][] memo) {
        if (n == 0 || W == 0)
            return 0;

        if (memo[n][W] != -1)
            return memo[n][W];

        int pick = 0;
        if (wt[n - 1] <= W)
            pick = val[n - 1] + knapsackRec(W - wt[n - 1], val, wt, n - 1, memo);

        int notPick = knapsackRec(W, val, wt, n - 1, memo);

        return memo[n][W] = Math.max(pick, notPick);
    }

    static int knapsack(int W, int val[], int wt[]) {
        int n = val.length;
        int[][] memo = new int[n + 1][W + 1];

        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j <= W; j++)
                memo[i][j] = -1;
        }

        return knapsackRec(W, val, wt, n, memo);
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n * W)
  • Space Complexity: O(n * W)
    Where n is number of items and W is knapsack capacity

Notes:

  • This top-down memoized recursion avoids repeated calculations compared to naive recursion.
  • Space can be optimized using bottom-up DP with 1D array if needed.
  • Handles large inputs efficiently within given constraints.

Problem Statement: 249¶

Job Sequencing Problem
You are given two arrays:

  • deadline[] → the last time by which each job can be completed.
  • profit[] → the profit earned from completing each job.

Each job takes 1 unit of time and only one job can be scheduled at a time.
Your goal is to schedule jobs such that:

  • The maximum number of jobs are completed within their deadlines.
  • The total profit is maximized.

📥 Input

  • deadline[]: integer array of size n
  • profit[]: integer array of size n

📤 Output

  • Return an array of two integers:
    1. Maximum number of jobs that can be completed
    2. Maximum total profit from the completed jobs

Example
Input:

deadline = \[2, 1, 2, 1, 3]
profit = \[100, 19, 27, 25, 15]

Output:

\[3, 142]

Explanation:
Jobs scheduled to maximize profit within deadlines:

  • Job with profit 100 at deadline 2
  • Job with profit 27 at deadline 2
  • Job with profit 15 at deadline 3
    Total profit = 100 + 27 + 15 = 142, 3 jobs done.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= n <= 10^5
  • 1 <= deadline[i] <= 10^5
  • 1 <= profit[i] <= 10^5

Goal:
Maximize number of jobs completed by their deadlines and maximize total profit earned.

🧠 Approach

  1. Pair Deadline with Profit:

    • Create a list of jobs where each job is represented as [deadline, profit].

  2. Sort by Deadline:

    • Sort the jobs based on increasing deadlines so earlier deadlines are prioritized.

  3. Use a Min-Heap:

    • Maintain a min-heap (priority queue) to keep track of the most profitable jobs that can fit into the available time.
    • If the size of the heap is less than the job's deadline, add the job's profit.
    • If the heap is full, and current job has higher profit than the minimum in heap, replace it.

  4. Count Jobs and Profit:

    • The size of the heap gives the number of jobs done.
    • The sum of elements in the heap gives the total profit.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Pair jobs (deadline, profit)
  • Sort jobs by deadline ascending
  • Use min-heap to track jobs with highest profits fitting into available slots
  • Replace lower profit jobs if better profit found
  • Calculate total jobs and profit
  • Return result

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function jobSequencing(deadline, profit):
jobs = \[(deadline\[i], profit\[i]) for i in range(n)]
sort jobs by deadline ascending
minHeap = empty priority queue

for job in jobs:
    if job.deadline > size(minHeap):
        minHeap.push(job.profit)
    else if minHeap.peek() < job.profit:
        minHeap.pop()
        minHeap.push(job.profit)

totalJobs = size(minHeap)
totalProfit = sum of all elements in minHeap
return [totalJobs, totalProfit]

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public ArrayList<Integer> jobSequencing(int[] deadline, int[] profit) {
        int n = deadline.length;
        ArrayList<Integer> ans = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(0, 0));

        List<int[]> jobs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            jobs.add(new int[]{deadline[i], profit[i]});
        }

        jobs.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0]));
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();

        for (int[] job : jobs) {
            if (job[0] > pq.size()) {
                pq.add(job[1]);
            } else if (!pq.isEmpty() && pq.peek() < job[1]) {
                pq.poll();
                pq.add(job[1]);
            }
        }

        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            ans.set(1, ans.get(1) + pq.poll());
            ans.set(0, ans.get(0) + 1);
        }

        return ans;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n log n)
    (due to sorting and heap operations)
  • Space Complexity: O(n)
    (for heap and job list)

Notes:

  • Sorting by deadline ensures jobs are scheduled as early as possible.
  • Min-heap helps efficiently track and replace lowest profit jobs when better options appear.
  • This greedy approach maximizes total profit while respecting deadlines.
  • Handles large inputs efficiently with O(n log n) complexity.

Problem Statement: 250¶

Middle Pattern
Given a string s of odd length, print characters in a specific rotated and growing pattern starting from the middle character.

Each step of the pattern:

  • Begins from the middle of the string.
  • Builds one character at a time in a circular (rotating) fashion.
  • Appends a $ after each constructed substring.
  • All outputs are printed in a single line, separated by a space.

📥 Input

  • A single string s of odd length.

📤 Output

  • A single line of output following the pattern described, ending with $ after each substring.

Example
Input:

s = "abcde"

Output:

c\$cd\$cde\$cdeab\$cdeabc\$

Constraints:

  • 1 <= s.length() <= 99
  • s.length() is odd

Goal:
Print substrings starting from the middle character, expanding circularly by one character each step, appending $ after each substring, all separated by space.

🧠 Approach

  1. Find the Middle Index:

    • Since the length is odd, the middle index is s.length() / 2.

  2. Circular Indexing:

    • Loop i from 0 to s.length() - 1
    • The current index becomes (i + mid) % s.length() to rotate over the string.

  3. Build & Print:

    • Accumulate characters in a string S from the calculated index.
    • Print S$ after each addition.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Find middle index
  • Initialize empty result string
  • Loop from 0 to n-1:
    • Calculate circular index (mid + i) % n
    • Append character at that index to substring
    • Print substring + $ with space

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function printPattern(s):
mid = length(s) // 2
substring = ""
n = length(s)
for i in 0 to n-1:
idx = (mid + i) % n
substring += s\[idx]
print substring + "\$ "

💻 Java Code

class GfG {
    // Method prints the given pattern in a single line
    void printPattern(String s) {
        String S = "";
        int mid = s.length() / 2;

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            if (i + mid > s.length() - 1) {
                S = S + s.charAt(i + mid - s.length());
            } else {
                S = S + s.charAt(i + mid);
            }
            System.out.print(S + "$" + " ");
        }
        return;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n^2) (due to repeated string concatenation)
  • Space Complexity: O(n) (for string accumulation)

Notes:

  • Circular indexing allows wrap-around on string ends.
  • String concatenation inside loop causes O(n^2) time complexity; can be optimized with StringBuilder.
  • Output format is space-separated substrings each ending with $.

Problem Statement: 251¶

Print Anagrams Together
Given an array of strings, your task is to return all groups of strings that are anagrams of each other.

📌 The strings in each group must be returned in the order they appear in the original array.

📥 Input

  • A string array arr[] of size n.

📤 Output

  • A list of lists (2D list), where each inner list contains a group of anagrams.
  • Strings in each group must appear in the same order as in the input.

Example
Input:

arr = \["cat", "tac", "dog", "god", "act"]

Output:

\[\["cat", "tac", "act"], \["dog", "god"]]

Constraints:

  • 1 <= n <= 10^5
  • 1 <= length of each string <= 100

🧠 Approach

  1. Sort the Characters in Each Word:

    • For each word, sort its characters to create a unique key for all its anagrams.

  2. Group Using a HashMap:

    • Use a HashMap (preferably a LinkedHashMap to preserve insertion order).
    • The key is the sorted string, and the value is a list of words that match that key.

  3. Collect and Return All Groups:

    • Return the values of the map as a list of lists.

Pseudocode:

map = LinkedHashMap\<String, List<String>>
for word in arr:
key = sort\_characters(word)
if key not in map:
map\[key] = new List
map\[key].add(word)
return map.values()

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public ArrayList<ArrayList<String>> anagrams(String[] arr) {
        // Use LinkedHashMap to preserve insertion order
        HashMap<String, ArrayList<String>> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        
        for (String word : arr) {
            char[] chars = word.toCharArray();
            Arrays.sort(chars);
            String key = new String(chars); // Sorted version as key

            // Create list if key doesn't exist
            map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>());
            map.get(key).add(word);
        }

        // Convert map values to list of lists
        return new ArrayList<>(map.values());
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n * k log k)
    (n: number of strings, k: max length of a string)
  • Space Complexity: O(n * k) for storing results and keys.

Notes:

  • Use LinkedHashMap to maintain the insertion order of groups based on first occurrence.
  • Sorting characters of each string is crucial to form the grouping key.
  • Grouping must preserve the order of strings within each group as they appear in the input.

Problem Statement: 252¶

Sum in a Matrix
You are given a 0-indexed 2D integer array nums. Initially, your score is 0. Perform the following operations until the matrix becomes empty:

  1. From each row, select the largest number and remove it.
    • If there is a tie, it does not matter which number is chosen.
  2. Among all the numbers removed in the current step, find the maximum value.
  3. Add this maximum value to your score.

🔁 Repeat until the matrix has no more elements.

Return the final score after all operations.

📥 Input

  • A 2D integer array nums[][] of size m x n.

📤 Output

  • An integer representing the total score after performing all operations.

Example

Input:

nums = \[
\[1, 2, 4],
\[3, 3, 1]
]

Step-by-step Process:

  • Sort each row:
    [[1, 2, 4], [1, 3, 3]]

  • Iteration 1 (last column): pick 4 and 3 → max = 4 → score = 4

  • Iteration 2 (second column): pick 2 and 3 → max = 3 → score = 7

  • Iteration 3 (first column): pick 1 and 1 → max = 1 → score = 8

Output:

8

Constraints

  • m == nums.length
  • n == nums[i].length for all 0 <= i < m
  • 1 <= m, n <= 50
  • 1 <= nums[i][j] <= 100

Goal:
Compute the total score after repeatedly removing the largest number from each row and adding the maximum among them.

🧠 Approach

  1. Sort Each Row in Ascending Order:

    • This allows us to always remove the largest remaining number from the end.

  2. Iterate Column-Wise from Right to Left:

    • For each column index from n-1 to 0, get the largest value among all rows at that column.

  3. Add the Column Max to Score:

    • This simulates picking the max of all popped values in that round.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

1. For each row in nums:
   a. Sort the row in ascending order.
2. Initialize score = 0
3. For col from n-1 to 0:
   a. maxVal = 0
   b. For each row:
   i. maxVal = max(maxVal, nums\[row]\[col])
   c. Add maxVal to score
4. Return score

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public int matrixSum(int[][] nums) {
        int m = nums.length;
        int n = nums[0].length;

        // Sort each row in ascending order
        for (int[] row : nums) {
            Arrays.sort(row);
        }

        int score = 0;

        // Traverse column by column from the last column
        for (int col = n - 1; col >= 0; col--) {
            int maxInCol = 0;
            for (int row = 0; row < m; row++) {
                maxInCol = Math.max(maxInCol, nums[row][col]);
            }
            score += maxInCol;
        }

        return score;   
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(m * n log n) due to sorting each of the m rows.
  • Space Complexity: O(1) extra space (in-place sorting).

Notes:

  • Sorting each row ensures the largest unremoved element is at the end.
  • Traversing columns from right to left simulates step-by-step removal from rows.

Problem Statement: 253¶

Group Anagrams
Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order.

📥 Input

  • An array of strings strs[].

📤 Output

  • A list of lists of strings, where each list contains all anagrams grouped together.

Example
Input:

strs = \["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"]

Output:

\[
\["eat","tea","ate"],
\["tan","nat"],
\["bat"]
]

Constraints:

  • 1 <= strs.length <= 10^4
  • 0 <= strs[i].length <= 100
  • strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.

Goal:
Group strings that are anagrams of each other into lists and return all such lists.

🧠 Approach

  1. Sort Each String:

    • Convert each string to a character array, sort it, and convert it back to a string. This sorted string will serve as a key.
    • Anagrams will have the same sorted string, so they can be grouped together.

  2. Use a HashMap:

    • Use a HashMap to store groups of anagrams. The key will be the sorted string, and the value will be the list of strings that are anagrams of each other.

  3. Add Original Strings to the Map:

    • For each string, get its sorted version and use it as the key to group the strings into the same anagram list.

  4. Return the Values:

    • After processing all strings, return the values of the map which contain the grouped anagrams.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

1. Initialize an empty HashMap
2. For each string s in strs:
   a. Sort the string to get a key
   b. Add s to map\[key]
3. Return all values from the map as a list of lists

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] strs) {
        Map<String, List<String>> map = new HashMap<>();

        // Iterate through each string in the array
        for (String s : strs) {
            // Convert string to char array, sort it, and convert back to string
            char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
            Arrays.sort(chars);
            String key = new String(chars); // this becomes the group ID for anagrams

            // Add the original string to the corresponding group
            map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(s);
        }

        // Return all grouped anagrams
        return new ArrayList<>(map.values());
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n * k log k) where n is the number of strings and k is the average length of the strings. Sorting each string takes O(k log k), and we perform this operation for each of the n strings.
  • Space Complexity: O(n * k) to store the strings and their anagram groups.

Notes:

  • Sorting the characters is key to identifying anagram groups.
  • HashMap ensures efficient grouping and retrieval.

Problem Statement: 254¶

Most Common Word
Given a string paragraph and a string array of the banned words banned, return the most frequent word that is not banned. It is guaranteed there is at least one word that is not banned, and that the answer is unique.

The words in the paragraph are case-insensitive and the answer should be returned in lowercase.

📥 Input

  • A string paragraph which contains words separated by spaces and punctuation marks.
  • A string array banned[] that contains words that should be ignored.

📤 Output

  • A string representing the most common word in paragraph that is not present in the banned list.

Example
Input:

paragraph = "Bob hit a ball, the hit BALL flew far after it was hit."
banned = \["hit"]

Output:

"ball"

Constraints:

  • 1 <= paragraph.length <= 1000
  • paragraph consists of English letters, space ' ', or one of the punctuation symbols !?',;..
  • 1 <= banned.length <= 100
  • 1 <= banned[i].length <= 10
  • The answer is guaranteed to be unique and not in the banned list.

Goal:
Return the lowercase version of the most frequent word that is not in the banned list.

🧠 Approach

  1. Normalize the Paragraph:

    • Convert the entire paragraph to lowercase.
    • Replace all non-letter characters with spaces, so only words remain.

  2. Split the Paragraph into Words:

    • After normalizing the string, split it into words using spaces as separators.

  3. Count Word Frequencies:

    • Use a HashMap to count the frequency of each word, excluding any words that appear in the banned list.

  4. Identify the Most Frequent Word:

    • Traverse the frequency map and track the word with the highest frequency that is not banned.

  5. Return the Most Common Word:

    • Return the word with the highest frequency after processing all words.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

1. Convert paragraph to lowercase
2. Replace punctuation with spaces
3. Split paragraph into words
4. Add banned words to a set
5. Use a hashmap to count frequency of non-banned words
6. Track the word with the highest frequency
7. Return that word

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public String mostCommonWord(String paragraph, String[] banned) {
        Set<String> bannedSet = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(banned));

        // Normalize paragraph: lowercase and replace all non-letter characters with space
        String normalized = paragraph.toLowerCase().replaceAll("[^a-z]", " ");
        String[] words = normalized.split("\\s+");

        // Count word frequencies excluding banned words
        Map<String, Integer> freqMap = new HashMap<>();
        for (String word : words) {
            if (!bannedSet.contains(word) && !word.isEmpty()) {
                freqMap.put(word, freqMap.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1);
            }
        }

        // Find the word with the maximum frequency
        String mostCommon = "";
        int maxFreq = 0;
        for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entry : freqMap.entrySet()) {
            if (entry.getValue() > maxFreq) {
                mostCommon = entry.getKey();
                maxFreq = entry.getValue();
            }
        }

        return mostCommon;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n) where n is the number of characters in the paragraph. We process each character, split the string into words, and count frequencies in a single pass.
  • Space Complexity: O(m) where m is the number of unique words in the paragraph, due to storing the word frequencies and the banned words.

Notes:

  • Using regex [^\a-z] helps to clean up the paragraph for word processing.
  • HashSet offers efficient lookup for banned words.
  • Ensures unique most frequent word is returned.

Problem Statement: 255¶

Check if the Sentence Is Pangram
A pangram is a sentence where every letter of the English alphabet appears at least once.

Given a string sentence containing only lowercase English letters, return true if the sentence is a pangram, or false otherwise.

📥 Input

  • A string sentence consisting of lowercase English letters (a-z).

📤 Output

  • A boolean value true if the sentence is a pangram, and false otherwise.

Example
Input:

sentence = "thequickbrownfoxjumpsoverthelazydog"

Output:

true

Constraints:

  • 1 <= sentence.length <= 1000
  • sentence consists only of lowercase English letters.

Goal:
Return true if the input sentence is a pangram (contains all 26 letters), otherwise return false.

🧠 Approach

  1. Track Seen Characters:

    • Create a boolean array of size 26 to track whether each letter of the alphabet has been encountered in the sentence.

  2. Mark Seen Characters:

    • Traverse the sentence and mark the corresponding index of each character in the boolean array as true (indicating the character has been seen).

  3. Check All Letters:

    • After processing the sentence, check if all positions in the boolean array are true. If any letter has not been encountered, return false.

  4. Return the Result:

    • If all positions are true, return true, indicating that the sentence contains every letter of the alphabet at least once.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

1. Initialize a boolean array of size 26 (for 'a' to 'z')
2. For each character in sentence:
   Mark corresponding index as true
3. Check if all 26 positions in the array are true
4. Return true if all seen, else false

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public boolean checkIfPangram(String sentence) {
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[26];

        for (char c : sentence.toCharArray()) {
            seen[c - 'a'] = true;
        }

        for (boolean b : seen) {
            if (!b) return false;
        }

        return true; 
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the length of the sentence. We traverse the sentence once and check the boolean array in linear time.
  • Space Complexity: O(1) as we are using a fixed-size boolean array of length 26, independent of the input size.

Notes:

  • This is a character-frequency tracking problem constrained to 26 lowercase letters.
  • Early return is possible if all 26 characters are found before end of sentence.

Problem Statement: 256¶

Matrix Diagonal Sum
Given a square matrix mat, return the sum of the matrix diagonals.
Only include the sum of all the elements on the primary diagonal and all the elements on the secondary diagonal that are not part of the primary diagonal.

📥 Input

  • A 2D integer array mat of size n x n, representing a square matrix.

📤 Output

  • An integer representing the sum of the primary and secondary diagonals of the matrix, excluding double-counted elements at the center if n is odd.

Example
Input:

mat = \[\[1,2,3],
\[4,5,6],
\[7,8,9]]

Output:

25

Constraints:

  • 1 <= mat.length <= 100
  • mat.length == mat[i].length
  • 1 <= mat[i][j] <= 100

Goal:
Return the total sum of elements from both the primary and secondary diagonals, subtracting the middle element once if double-counted.

🧠 Approach

  1. Traverse Diagonals:

    • The primary diagonal consists of elements where the row and column indices are equal, i.e., mat[i][i].
    • The secondary diagonal consists of elements where the row index and column index sum to n - 1, i.e., mat[i][n - 1 - i].

  2. Avoid Double Counting:

    • If the matrix size n is odd, the center element will be counted twice (once in the primary and once in the secondary diagonal), so subtract it once.

  3. Return the Sum:

    • Add the elements from both diagonals, ensuring not to double-count the center element if n is odd.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

1. Initialize sum = 0
2. For i from 0 to n-1:

   * Add mat\[i]\[i] (primary diagonal)
   * Add mat\[i]\[n - 1 - i] (secondary diagonal)
3. If n is odd:

   * Subtract mat\[n / 2]\[n / 2] once to avoid double-count
4. Return sum

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public int diagonalSum(int[][] mat) {
        int n = mat.length;
        int sum = 0;

        // Traverse both diagonals
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            sum += mat[i][i]; // Primary diagonal
            sum += mat[i][n - 1 - i]; // Secondary diagonal
        }

        // If the matrix size is odd, subtract the center element once
        if (n % 2 == 1) {
            sum -= mat[n / 2][n / 2];
        }

        return sum;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the size of one dimension of the matrix. We traverse the matrix once.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), as we only use a constant amount of extra space.

Notes:

  • For even n, no center element is shared, so no adjustment needed.
  • This is a direct traversal problem and requires simple indexing logic.

Problem Statement: 257¶

Solve the Sudoku
Given an incomplete Sudoku configuration in terms of a 9x9 2-D integer square matrix, mat[][], the task is to solve the Sudoku. It is guaranteed that the input Sudoku will have exactly one solution.

A Sudoku solution must satisfy all of the following rules:

  1. Each of the digits 1-9 must occur exactly once in each row.
  2. Each of the digits 1-9 must occur exactly once in each column.
  3. Each of the digits 1-9 must occur exactly once in each of the 9 3x3 sub-boxes of the grid.

Note:

  • Zeros represent blanks to be filled with numbers 1-9, while non-zero cells are fixed and cannot be changed.

📥 Input

  • A 9x9 2D array mat representing the Sudoku board. The array contains integers from 0 to 9, where 0 represents an empty cell that needs to be filled.

📤 Output

  • The function should modify the input matrix mat in-place to represent the solved Sudoku.

Example
Input:

mat = {
{5,3,0,0,7,0,0,0,0},
{6,0,0,1,9,5,0,0,0},
{0,9,8,0,0,0,0,6,0},
{8,0,0,0,6,0,0,0,3},
{4,0,0,8,0,3,0,0,1},
{7,0,0,0,2,0,0,0,6},
{0,6,0,0,0,0,2,8,0},
{0,0,0,4,1,9,0,0,5},
{0,0,0,0,8,0,0,7,9}
};

Output:

mat (modified in-place) will contain the valid Sudoku solution.

Constraints:

  • The input board is a 9x9 grid of integers.
  • 0 <= mat[i][j] <= 9
  • The input puzzle is guaranteed to have a unique solution.

Goal:
Modify the given 9x9 board in-place to produce a valid completed Sudoku grid.

🧠 Approach

  1. Backtracking:

    • The approach uses backtracking to fill the Sudoku board.
    • Traverse through each cell, and whenever an empty cell (0) is found, try filling it with numbers from 1 to 9.
    • For each number, check if placing it in the current cell follows the Sudoku rules (i.e., no repetition in the row, column, or 3x3 sub-grid).
    • If a valid number is found, proceed with the next empty cell. If no number fits, backtrack and remove the previously placed number.
    • Continue this process until the board is completely filled.

  2. Validation:

    • A helper function isValid checks whether placing a given number in a specific cell violates the Sudoku rules:
      • The number should not already exist in the same row.
      • The number should not already exist in the same column.
      • The number should not already exist in the 3x3 sub-box.

  3. Termination:

    • If all cells are filled correctly, the board will be solved, and the function will return true.
    • If no valid placement is possible, the function backtracks.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function solveSudoku(mat):
solve()

function solve():
for row in 0..8:
for col in 0..8:
if mat\[row]\[col] == 0:
for num in 1..9:
if isValid(mat, row, col, num):
mat\[row]\[col] = num
if solve():
return true
mat\[row]\[col] = 0
return false
return true

function isValid(mat, row, col, num):
if num exists in mat\[row]\[*] or mat\[*]\[col] or 3x3 grid of mat\[row]\[col]:
return false
return true

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    // Function to find a solved Sudoku.
    static void solveSudoku(int[][] mat) {
        // code here
        solve(mat);
    }

    // Backtracking function to solve the Sudoku.
    private static boolean solve(int[][] mat) {
        for (int row = 0; row < 9; row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < 9; col++) {
                if (mat[row][col] == 0) { // If the cell is empty
                    for (int num = 1; num <= 9; num++) { // Try numbers from 1 to 9
                        if (isValid(mat, row, col, num)) {
                            mat[row][col] = num; // Place the number

                            // Recursively solve the rest of the board
                            if (solve(mat)) {
                                return true;
                            }

                            mat[row][col] = 0; // Backtrack if no solution found
                        }
                    }
                    return false; // If no valid number can be placed, return false
                }
            }
        }
        return true; // Sudoku solved
    }

    // Function to check if placing 'num' at mat[row][col] is valid
    private static boolean isValid(int[][] mat, int row, int col, int num) {
        // Check the row and column
        for (int i = 0; i < 9; i++) {
            if (mat[row][i] == num || mat[i][col] == num) {
                return false;
            }
        }

        // Check the 3x3 sub-grid
        int boxStartRow = row - row % 3;
        int boxStartCol = col - col % 3;
        for (int i = boxStartRow; i < boxStartRow + 3; i++) {
            for (int j = boxStartCol; j < boxStartCol + 3; j++) {
                if (mat[i][j] == num) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
        }

        return true; // The number is valid
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(9^(n^2)), where n is the size of the board (9x9). In the worst case, we might need to try each number for each cell.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), as the solution modifies the board in-place and does not use extra space except for a few variables.

Notes:

  • This classic backtracking problem explores depth-first possibilities and uses constraints to prune invalid branches early.
  • Efficiency can be improved by using auxiliary data structures (e.g., boolean arrays for row/column/box tracking), but the provided solution is straightforward and correct.

Problem Statement: 258¶

Check if frequencies can be equal

Given a string s which contains only lower alphabetic characters, check if it is possible to remove at most one character from this string in such a way that the frequency of each distinct character becomes the same in the string. Return true if it is possible to do so, otherwise return false.

📥 Input

  • A string s of lowercase English letters.

📤 Output

  • Return true if it is possible to remove at most one character such that the frequency of each distinct character becomes the same in the string. Otherwise, return false.

Example
Input: "aabbcc"
Output: true
Explanation: Remove one 'a', 'b', or 'c' to make all remaining character frequencies equal to 2.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= s.length <= 10^5
  • s consists only of lowercase English letters.

Goal:
Check if by removing at most one character from the string, the frequencies of all distinct characters can become equal.

🧠 Approach

  1. Frequency Calculation:

    • First, calculate the frequency of each character in the string.
    • The problem boils down to checking if, after removing one character (or none), all characters can have the same frequency.

  2. Check for Equal Frequencies:

    • If the frequency of all characters is already the same, return true.

  3. One Removal Check:

    • Iterate through each character. For each character that has a non-zero frequency, temporarily reduce its frequency by 1, and check if all frequencies are now the same. If so, return true.

  4. Edge Case:

    • If the string is already balanced, no removal is needed, so return true.

  5. Efficiency:

    • We iterate over all characters of the string once to calculate the frequencies.
    • Then we check if removing one character can make the frequencies equal, which requires iterating through the 26 possible characters.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  1. Count frequency of each character.
  2. Check if all frequencies are equal → return true.
  3. Try reducing each frequency by 1 and check if the rest become equal → return true if possible.
  4. Else, return false.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function sameFreq(s):
freq = array of size 26 initialized to 0
for each character c in s:
increment freq\[c - 'a']

if all frequencies in freq (ignoring 0s) are the same:
    return true

for i from 0 to 25:
    if freq[i] > 0:
        decrement freq[i]
        if all frequencies (ignoring 0s) are equal:
            return true
        increment freq[i] // restore

return false

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    static final int M = 26;

    // Helper function to get index for a character
    static int getIdx(char ch) {
        return (ch - 'a');
    }

    // Helper function to check if all frequencies are the same
    static boolean allSame(int freq[], int N) {
        int same = 0;
        int i;
        // Find a non-zero frequency to compare with others
        for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
            if (freq[i] > 0) {
                same = freq[i];
                break;
            }
        }

        // Check if all frequencies are the same
        for (int j = i + 1; j < N; j++)
            if (freq[j] > 0 && freq[j] != same)
                return false;

        return true;
    }

    // Main function to check if frequencies can be made equal by removing at most one character
    boolean sameFreq(String str) {
        int l = str.length();
        int[] freq = new int[M]; // Frequency array for 26 characters

        // Count frequency of each character
        for (int i = 0; i < l; i++)
            freq[getIdx(str.charAt(i))]++;

        // Check if all frequencies are already the same
        if (allSame(freq, M))
            return true;

        // Try removing one character and check if frequencies become equal
        for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; c++) {
            int i = getIdx(c);

            // If this character has non-zero frequency, remove one occurrence and check
            if (freq[i] > 0) {
                freq[i]--;

                // Check if frequencies are now the same
                if (allSame(freq, M))
                    return true;

                freq[i]++; // Restore the frequency back if it doesn't work
            }
        }

        return false; // If no solution is found
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n + 26), where n is the length of the string. The first pass is to count the frequencies and the second pass is to check for removal of one character.
  • Space Complexity: O(26) for storing the frequency of each character (fixed size of the alphabet).

Notes:

  • Frequencies are considered equal if all non-zero counts match.
  • Removing one character can mean reducing any one character’s frequency by one.

Problem Statement: 259¶

Return Two Prime Numbers

Given an even number n (greater than 2), return two prime numbers whose sum will be equal to the given number. There are several combinations possible. Print only the pair whose minimum value is the smallest among all the minimum values of pairs and print the minimum element first.

Note: A solution will always exist based on Goldbach's conjecture, which states that every even integer greater than 2 can be expressed as the sum of two primes.

📥 Input

  • An even integer n (greater than 2).

📤 Output

  • Return a pair of prime numbers whose sum equals n where the minimum number in the pair is the smallest possible among all pairs.

Example
Input: n = 74
Output: [3, 71]
Explanation: 3 and 71 are both prime and 3 + 71 = 74. No smaller minimum value pair exists.

Constraints:

  • n is an even integer such that n > 2
  • It is guaranteed that a solution exists.

Goal:
Find and return a pair of prime numbers whose sum equals the given even number n, such that the smaller number in the pair is the smallest possible.

🧠 Approach

  1. Prime Sieve (Sieve of Eratosthenes):

    • Use the sieve algorithm to generate all prime numbers up to n.
    • Mark all numbers as prime initially and eliminate non-prime numbers by marking multiples of each prime starting from 2.

  2. Finding the Pair:

    • Iterate through numbers from 2 to n/2.
    • For each number i, check if both i and n - i are prime. If they are, return the pair (i, n - i).

  3. Efficiency:

    • The sieve runs in O(n log log n) time, which is efficient for finding all primes up to n.
    • The pair search is linear in time, iterating through numbers up to n/2.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  1. Generate prime numbers up to n using sieve.
  2. Loop i from 2 to n / 2:
    • If i and n - i are both prime, return [i, n - i].
  3. Stop at the first such pair.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function sieve(n):
create array isPrime\[0..n] and set all to true
isPrime\[0] = isPrime\[1] = false
for i from 2 to sqrt(n):
if isPrime\[i]:
for j from i\*i to n step i:
isPrime\[j] = false
return isPrime

function primeDivision(n):
isPrime = sieve(n)
for i from 2 to n / 2:
if isPrime\[i] and isPrime\[n - i]:
return \[i, n - i]
return \[]

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    // Function to generate primes up to n using Sieve of Eratosthenes
    static boolean[] sieve(int n) {
        boolean[] isPrime = new boolean[n + 1]; 
        Arrays.fill(isPrime, true); 
     
        isPrime[0] = isPrime[1] = false;  // 0 and 1 are not prime numbers

        for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) {
            if (isPrime[i]) {
                // Mark multiples of i as non-prime
                for (int j = i * i; j <= n; j += i) {
                    isPrime[j] = false; 
                }
            }
        }
        return isPrime; 
    }

    // Function to find two prime numbers whose sum equals n
    static List<Integer> primeDivision(int n) {
        boolean[] isPrime = sieve(n);  // Get prime numbers up to n

        // Check for pairs of primes that sum to n
        for (int i = 2; i <= n / 2; i++) {
            if (isPrime[i] && isPrime[n - i]) {
                return Arrays.asList(i, n - i);  // Return the pair
            }
        }
  
        return new ArrayList<>();  // Return empty if no solution (should never happen)
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n log log n) for the sieve of Eratosthenes and O(n) for finding the pair.
  • Space Complexity: O(n) for storing prime information.

Notes:

  • Based on Goldbach's conjecture, a solution will always exist for even n > 2.
  • The earliest valid pair in the loop guarantees the smallest minimum value.

Problem Statement: 260¶

Longest Palindromic Substring

Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s. A substring of string s is a contiguous sequence of characters within a string, i.e., s[i..j] where 0 ≤ i ≤ j < len(s). A palindromic string is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards. More formally, s is a palindrome if reverse(s) = s. If there are multiple longest palindromic substrings, return the substring with the least starting index.

📥 Input

  • A string s of length n (1 ≤ n ≤ 1000).

📤 Output

  • The longest palindromic substring of s.

Example
Input: "babad"
Output: "bab"
Explanation: "bab" and "aba" are both longest palindromic substrings, but "bab" appears first.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000
  • The string s consists of lowercase and/or uppercase English letters.

Goal:
Return the longest palindromic substring in the input string s. If multiple longest substrings exist, return the one with the smallest starting index.

🧠 Approach The idea is to check for all possible substrings and expand around the center to find the longest palindrome. We will use the following approach:

  1. Expand Around Center:

    • Each palindrome can be expanded from a center. There are two kinds of centers:
      • One character as the center (for odd-length palindromes).
      • Two consecutive characters as the center (for even-length palindromes).
    • For each center, expand left and right to check if the string is a palindrome.

  2. Track Maximum Length:

    • For each valid palindrome found, track the maximum length and update the result if it's longer than the previously found palindrome.

  3. Return the Longest Palindrome:

    • The algorithm will return the longest palindromic substring based on the maximum length and starting index.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • For each index i in the string:
    • Expand around center i for odd-length palindromes.
    • Expand around centers i and i+1 for even-length palindromes.
    • Update maximum length and starting index if a longer palindrome is found.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

initialize start = 0, maxLen = 1
for i in 0 to n-1:
for j in \[0,1]:  // j=0 odd center, j=1 even center
low = i
high = i + j
while low >= 0 and high < n and s\[low] == s\[high]:
currLen = high - low + 1
if currLen > maxLen:
start = low
maxLen = currLen
low--
high++
return substring(s, start, start + maxLen)

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    String longestPalindrome(String s) {
        // code here
        int n = s.length();
        if (n == 0) return "";

        int start = 0, maxLen = 1;

        // Loop through each character in the string
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

            // Check for odd-length and even-length palindromes
            for (int j = 0; j <= 1; j++) {
                int low = i;
                int high = i + j; // Start with the center of the palindrome

                // Expand around the center
                while (low >= 0 && high < n && s.charAt(low) == s.charAt(high)) {
                    int currLen = high - low + 1; // Current palindrome length
                    if (currLen > maxLen) {
                        start = low; // Update start index of the longest palindrome
                        maxLen = currLen; // Update max length
                    }
                    low--;
                    high++;
                }
            }
        }

        return s.substring(start, start + maxLen); // Return the longest palindrome
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n^2) where n is the length of the string, as we are expanding from each possible center.
  • Space Complexity: O(1) as we are using only a few extra variables to store the result.

Notes:

  • Handles both odd and even length palindromes by considering one or two center characters.
  • Returns the earliest longest palindrome if multiple substrings share maximum length.

Problem Statement: 261¶

Spirally Traversing a Matrix

You are given a rectangular matrix mat[][] of size n x m, and your task is to return an array while traversing the matrix in spiral form.

📥 Input

  • A 2D array mat with n rows and m columns (1 ≤ n, m ≤ 1000).
  • The matrix contains integers.

📤 Output

  • A list of integers that represent the elements of the matrix in spiral order.

Example
Input:

mat = \[
\[1, 2, 3],
\[4, 5, 6],
\[7, 8, 9]
]

Output: [1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 8, 7, 4, 5]

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n, m ≤ 1000
  • Elements of the matrix can be any integers (positive, negative, zero).

Goal:
Return an array containing the elements of the matrix traversed in spiral order starting from the top-left corner.

🧠 Approach The approach to solving the problem involves simulating the spiral traversal in four directions:

  1. Left to Right: Traverse the topmost row from left to right.
  2. Top to Bottom: Traverse the rightmost column from top to bottom.
  3. Right to Left: Traverse the bottommost row from right to left (if there are still rows).
  4. Bottom to Top: Traverse the leftmost column from bottom to top (if there are still columns).

After each traversal, we adjust the boundaries of the matrix to move inward and continue the process until all elements have been visited.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Initialize pointers: top=0, bottom=n-1, left=0, right=m-1
  • While top <= bottom and left <= right:
    • Traverse from left to right along top row; increment top
    • Traverse from top to bottom along right column; decrement right
    • Traverse from right to left along bottom row if top <= bottom; decrement bottom
    • Traverse from bottom to top along left column if left <= right; increment left

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

initialize top = 0, bottom = n - 1
initialize left = 0, right = m - 1
initialize result list res = \[]

while top <= bottom and left <= right:
for i in left to right:
res.add(mat\[top]\[i])
top += 1

for i in top to bottom:
    res.add(mat[i][right])
right -= 1

if top <= bottom:
    for i in right down to left:
        res.add(mat[bottom][i])
    bottom -= 1

if left <= right:
    for i in bottom down to top:
        res.add(mat[i][left])
    left += 1

return res

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    // Function to return a list of integers denoting spiral traversal of matrix.
    public ArrayList<Integer> spirallyTraverse(int mat[][]) {
        // code here
        int m = mat.length;
        int n = mat[0].length;

        ArrayList<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();

        int top = 0, bottom = m - 1, left = 0, right = n - 1;

        while (top <= bottom && left <= right) {

            // Traverse from left to right along the topmost row
            for (int i = left; i <= right; ++i) {
                res.add(mat[top][i]);
            }
            top++;

            // Traverse from top to bottom along the rightmost column
            for (int i = top; i <= bottom; ++i) {
                res.add(mat[i][right]);
            }
            right--;

            if (top <= bottom) {
                // Traverse from right to left along the bottommost row
                for (int i = right; i >= left; --i) {
                    res.add(mat[bottom][i]);
                }
                bottom--;
            }

            if (left <= right) {
                // Traverse from bottom to top along the leftmost column
                for (int i = bottom; i >= top; --i) {
                    res.add(mat[i][left]);
                }
                left++;
            }
        }

        return res;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n * m) where n is the number of rows and m is the number of columns, as we are visiting each element exactly once.
  • Space Complexity: O(1) excluding the space for the result, as we are using a few extra variables for boundary management.

Notes:

  • The traversal ensures no element is visited more than once.
  • Adjusting boundaries after each directional traversal prevents overlaps.
  • Works correctly for non-square matrices.

Problem Statement: 262¶

Coin Change (Count Ways)

Given an integer array coins[] representing different denominations of currency and an integer sum, find the number of ways you can make the sum by using different combinations from coins[].
Note: Assume that you have an infinite supply of each type of coin. Therefore, you can use any coin as many times as you want.
Answers are guaranteed to fit into a 32-bit integer.

📥 Input

  • An integer array coins[] of size n (1 ≤ n ≤ 100).
  • An integer sum (1 ≤ sum ≤ 10000), representing the target sum.

📤 Output

  • The number of ways to make the given sum using any combination of the coins.

Example
Input:

coins = \[1, 2, 3], sum = 4

Output: 4
Explanation: The four ways to make sum 4 are:

  • 1+1+1+1
  • 1+1+2
  • 1+3
  • 2+2

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 100
  • 1 ≤ sum ≤ 10000
  • Coins values are positive integers.

Goal:
Find the total number of distinct combinations (order does not matter) of coins that sum up to the target value.

🧠 Approach This problem can be solved using Dynamic Programming. We maintain a dp[] array where dp[i] represents the number of ways to make the sum i using the available coins.

Steps:

  1. Initialize dp[0] to 1 since there is one way to make sum 0, which is by choosing no coins.
  2. Loop through each coin, and for each coin, update the dp[] array for all sums from the coin's value up to the target sum.
  3. After processing all the coins, dp[sum] will contain the number of ways to make the sum using the available coins.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Initialize dp array of size sum+1 with zeros; set dp[0] = 1
  • For each coin in coins:
    • For j from coin value to sum:
      • Update dp[j] += dp[j - coin]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

initialize dp array of size sum + 1 with 0
dp\[0] = 1

for each coin in coins:
for j from coin to sum:
dp\[j] = dp\[j] + dp\[j - coin]

return dp\[sum]

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public int count(int coins[], int sum) {
        // code here.
        int n = coins.length;
      
        int[] dp = new int[sum + 1];

        dp[0] = 1;  // There is 1 way to make sum 0 (by selecting no coins)

        // For each coin, update the dp array for all sums from coin to sum
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            for (int j = coins[i]; j <= sum; j++)
                dp[j] += dp[j - coins[i]];
                
        return dp[sum];  // Return the number of ways to make the given sum
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n * sum), where n is the number of coins, and sum is the target sum. This is because we update the dp[] array for each coin.
  • Space Complexity: O(sum) because we only need a 1D dp[] array to store results for sums from 0 to sum.

Notes:

  • Uses a 1D DP approach optimized for space.
  • Order of coins does not matter, so combinations like (1,2) and (2,1) are counted once.
  • Infinite supply of coins assumed, so coin can be reused multiple times.

Problem Statement: 263¶

Longest Palindrome in a String

Given a string s, your task is to find the longest palindromic substring within s. A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within a string, defined as s[i...j] where 0 ≤ i ≤ j < len(s). A palindrome is a string that reads the same forward and backward. More formally, s is a palindrome if reverse(s) == s.

Note: If there are multiple palindromic substrings with the same length, return the first occurrence of the longest palindromic substring from left to right.

📥 Input

  • A string s of length n (1 ≤ n ≤ 1000), consisting of English letters (lowercase and uppercase).

📤 Output

  • The longest palindromic substring in the string s.

Example
Input:

s = "babad"

Output:

"bab"

Explanation:
Both "bab" and "aba" are palindromic substrings of length 3, but "bab" appears first.

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000
  • String consists of uppercase and lowercase English letters.

Goal:
Return the longest palindromic substring. If multiple longest substrings exist, return the first one by starting index.

🧠 Approach To find the longest palindromic substring, we can use an expand-around-center approach. This approach considers each character (or pair of characters) as a potential center of a palindrome and expands outwards to check if the substring remains a palindrome.

Steps:

  1. Initialize variables start and maxLen to track the starting index and the length of the longest palindromic substring found.
  2. Iterate through each character of the string:
    • Treat each character (and each pair of adjacent characters) as the center of a potential palindrome.
    • Expand outward from the center while the substring is a palindrome.
  3. Update the start index and maxLen when a longer palindrome is found.
  4. Return the longest palindromic substring from the start index with maxLen length.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • For each character in the string, consider it as the center for odd-length palindromes.
  • For each pair of adjacent characters, consider them as the center for even-length palindromes.
  • Expand outwards from the center(s) and check palindrome validity.
  • Update max length and starting index when longer palindrome is found.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

start = 0, maxLen = 1
for i in 0 to n-1:
for j in \[0,1]:  // j=0 odd-length, j=1 even-length centers
low = i
high = i + j
while low >= 0 and high < n and s\[low] == s\[high]:
currLen = high - low + 1
if currLen > maxLen:
start = low
maxLen = currLen
low -= 1
high += 1
return substring(s, start, start + maxLen)

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    static String longestPalindrome(String s) {
        // code here
        int n = s.length();
        if (n == 0) return "";

        int start = 0, maxLen = 1;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

            for (int j = 0; j <= 1; j++) {
                int low = i;
                int high = i + j; 

                while (low >= 0 && high < n && s.charAt(low) == s.charAt(high)) {
                    int currLen = high - low + 1;
                    if (currLen > maxLen) {
                        start = low;
                        maxLen = currLen;
                    }
                    low--;
                    high++;
                }
            }
        }

        return s.substring(start, start + maxLen);
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n^2), where n is the length of the string. We check each character and expand around it in both directions, which takes O(n) time per center.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), as we only use a few extra variables for tracking the result.

Notes:

  • Case sensitive matching.
  • Uses expand-around-center method for efficient palindrome search.
  • If string length is zero, returns empty string.

Problem Statement: 264¶

Merge Without Extra Space

Given two sorted arrays a[] and b[] of size n and m respectively, the task is to merge them in sorted order without using any extra space. Modify a[] so that it contains the first n elements and modify b[] so that it contains the last m elements.

📥 Input

  • Two sorted arrays a[] and b[] of sizes n and m respectively.

📤 Output

  • Merge the two arrays in sorted order without using any extra space. After merging, modify a[] and b[] to hold the first n and last m elements, respectively.

Example
Input:

a = \[1, 4, 7, 8, 10]
b = \[2, 3, 9]

Output:

a = \[1, 2, 3, 4, 7]
b = \[8, 9, 10]

Explanation:
After merging without extra space, the first n smallest elements are in a[] and the rest in b[].

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n, m ≤ 10^6 (array sizes)
  • Arrays a[] and b[] are initially sorted.

Goal:
Merge two sorted arrays without using extra space, modifying the input arrays in place.

🧠 Approach

  1. Two Pointer Technique:

    • Initialize two pointers, i and j. Pointer i will start at the end of array a[] (last element), and pointer j will start at the beginning of array b[] (first element).

  2. Compare and Swap:

    • Compare a[i] and b[j]. If a[i] is smaller than b[j], then no change is needed for a[i]. Otherwise, swap the values of a[i] and b[j] to maintain the sorted order.
    • After swapping, decrement i and increment j to continue comparing the next elements.

  3. Sort the Arrays:

    • Once the pointers have traversed both arrays, sort both arrays a[] and b[] to ensure that both are in sorted order.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start with pointers at end of a[] and start of b[].
  • Swap elements if a[i] > b[j].
  • Move pointers accordingly until no more swaps needed.
  • Sort both arrays.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

i = n-1
j = 0
while i >= 0 and j < m:
if a\[i] > b\[j]:
swap a\[i], b\[j]
i -= 1
j += 1
else:
i -= 1
sort a\[]
sort b\[]

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    // Function to merge the arrays.
    public void mergeArrays(int a[], int b[]) {
        // code here
        int i = a.length - 1, j = 0;

        while (i >= 0 && j < b.length) {
            if (a[i] < b[j])
                i--;
            else {
                int temp = b[j];
                b[j] = a[i];
                a[i] = temp;
                i--;
                j++;
            }
        }

        Arrays.sort(a);
        Arrays.sort(b);
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n log n + m log m), where n is the size of array a[] and m is the size of array b[]. This is because we sort both arrays after modifying them.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), as we are not using any extra space apart from the input arrays.

Notes:

  • The method relies on sorting after swapping to restore order.
  • No extra array or data structure is used, fulfilling the space constraint.
  • Sorting after swapping ensures final arrays are sorted.

Problem Statement: 265¶

Snake and Ladder Problem

Given a 5x6 snakes and ladders board, find the minimum number of dice throws required to reach the destination or last cell (30th cell) from the source (1st cell).

You are given an integer N denoting the total number of snakes and ladders and an array arr[] of size 2*N where 2i and (2i + 1)th values denote the starting and ending point respectively of the ith snake or ladder. The board looks like the following:

Note: Assume that you have complete control over the 6-sided dice. No ladder starts from the 1st cell.

📥 Input

  • An integer N denoting the total number of snakes and ladders.
  • An array arr[] of size 2*N where arr[2*i] and arr[2*i + 1] represent the start and end of the ith snake or ladder.

📤 Output

  • Return the minimum number of dice throws required to reach the destination (cell 30) from the source (cell 1).

Example
Input:

N = 3
arr = \[3, 22, 5, 8, 11, 26]

Output:

3

Explanation:
Minimum dice throws needed to reach from cell 1 to 30 considering given snakes and ladders.

Constraints:

  • Board size fixed at 30 cells (5x6).
  • 1 ≤ N ≤ 15 (total snakes and ladders).
  • No ladder starts from cell 1.

🧠 Approach

  1. Representation of the Board:

    • Use an array board[] of size 30 to represent the board where the value -1 means no snake or ladder.
    • For each snake or ladder, populate the board[] such that board[start] = end.

  2. Breadth-First Search (BFS):

    • Treat each cell as a node and moves from one cell to another as edges.
    • Use BFS to find the shortest path from the starting point (cell 1) to the destination (cell 30).
    • For each dice throw (i.e., moving from a cell to another), check if a snake or ladder exists and update the cell accordingly.

  3. Queue and Visited Array:

    • Use a queue to explore the board and keep track of the visited cells to avoid revisiting them.

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

Initialize board\[] with -1
For each snake or ladder (start, end):
board\[start-1] = end-1

Create a queue and visited\[] array
Enqueue the first cell (0) with distance 0
Mark visited\[0] = true

While queue not empty:
Dequeue current cell
If current cell == last cell (29), return distance
For dice throw from 1 to 6:
Calculate next cell
If not visited:
Mark visited
If board\[next] != -1, move to board\[next]
Enqueue next cell with distance+1

💻 Java Code

class Solution{
    static class qentry {
        int v; 
        int dist;
    }

    static int minThrow(int N, int move[]){
        int boardSize = 30;
        int[] board = new int[boardSize];

        // Initialize the board
        for (int i = 0; i < boardSize; i++) {
            board[i] = -1;
        }

        // Populate the board with snakes and ladders
        for (int i = 0; i < 2 * N; i += 2) {
            int start = move[i] - 1;
            int end = move[i + 1] - 1;
            board[start] = end;
        }

        // Initialize the visited array and the queue
        boolean[] visited = new boolean[boardSize];
        Queue<qentry> q = new LinkedList<>();
        qentry start = new qentry();
        start.v = 0;
        start.dist = 0;
        visited[0] = true;
        q.add(start);

        // BFS traversal
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            qentry curr = q.poll();
            int v = curr.v;

            if (v == boardSize - 1) {
                return curr.dist;  // Found the destination
            }

            // Try all dice throws
            for (int i = 1; i <= 6 && (v + i) < boardSize; i++) {
                int next = v + i;

                if (!visited[next]) {
                    visited[next] = true;
                    qentry nextEntry = new qentry();

                    // If a snake or ladder is present, move accordingly
                    nextEntry.v = (board[next] != -1) ? board[next] : next;
                    nextEntry.dist = curr.dist + 1;

                    q.add(nextEntry);
                }
            }
        }

        return -1; // No solution found (should not happen as a solution always exists)
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(N + 6 * boardSize), where boardSize is the total number of cells (30) and N is the number of snakes and ladders.
  • Space Complexity: O(boardSize) for storing the board and visited array.

Additional Notes:

  • The dice can roll values from 1 to 6.
  • BFS ensures shortest path (minimum dice throws) is found.
  • Board cells are zero-indexed internally but problem statement uses 1-based indexing.

Problem Statement: 266¶

Sorted Insert for Circular Linked List
