Given a sorted circular linked list, the task is to insert a new node in this circular list so that it remains a sorted circular linked list.

📥 Input

  • A circular linked list head, where head is the first node of the list.
  • An integer data which represents the value to be inserted in the list.

📤 Output

  • Return the updated circular linked list after inserting the new node in sorted order.

Example
Input:

head = \[1 -> 3 -> 4 -> (back to 1)], data = 2

Output:

\[1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> (back to 1)]

Explanation:
The new node with value 2 is inserted between 1 and 3, maintaining the sorted circular order.

Constraints:

  • The circular linked list is sorted in ascending order.
  • data can be any integer value.
  • The list may be empty (head == null).

Edge Cases:

  • Empty list (create a single node pointing to itself).
  • All nodes have the same value.
  • Inserting the largest value (insert at the end before head).

🧠 Approach

  1. Handle Empty List:

    • If the circular linked list is empty (head == null), create a new node and make its next point to itself.

  2. Inserting at the Beginning:

    • If the data is less than or equal to the head node’s data, find the last node of the list (the node whose next points to head) and insert the new node before the head.

  3. Inserting in the Middle or End:

    • Traverse through the list, checking each node’s value and comparing it with the data.
    • Insert the new node between two nodes such that the list remains sorted.

  4. Circular Structure:

    • Ensure that after insertion, the last node’s next points to the head, maintaining the circular structure of the list.

Pseudocode:

If head == null:
create newNode pointing to itself
return newNode

If data <= head.data:
Find last node (node whose next is head)
Insert newNode before head
return newNode (new head)

Traverse list starting from head:
if curr.data < data <= curr.next.data:
Insert newNode between curr and curr.next
return head

Insert newNode after last node (before head)
return head

💻 Java Code

class Solution {
    public Node sortedInsert(Node head, int data) {
        Node newNode = new Node(data);
        
        // Case 1: If the list is empty
        if (head == null) {
            newNode.next = newNode;
            return newNode;
        }

        Node curr = head;
        Node nextToCurr = head.next;

        // Case 2: If the data is smaller or equal to the head data, insert at the beginning
        if (data <= head.data) {
            Node lastNode = head;
            while (lastNode.next != head) {
                lastNode = lastNode.next;
            }
            newNode.next = head;
            lastNode.next = newNode;
            return newNode;
        }

        // Case 3: Traverse and find the correct position for the new node
        while (curr.next != head) {
            if (curr.data < data && nextToCurr.data >= data) {
                newNode.next = curr.next;
                curr.next = newNode;
                return head;
            } else {
                curr = curr.next;
                nextToCurr = nextToCurr.next;
            }
        }

        // If the new node is to be inserted at the end
        newNode.next = head;
        curr.next = newNode;
        return head;
    }
}

⏱️ Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the circular linked list. We may need to traverse the entire list in the worst case.
  • Space Complexity: O(1) as we are only using a constant amount of extra space.

Additional Notes:

  • When inserting a new smallest value, the new node becomes the new head.
  • For equal values, the new node is inserted before the first node with a greater or equal value.

Problem Statement: 267¶

Distinct Permutations of the String Given a string s, the task is to return all unique permutations of the given string in lexicographically sorted order.

A permutation is the rearrangement of all the elements of a string.

📥 Input

  • A single string s consisting of uppercase/lowercase alphabetic characters.

📤 Output

  • A list of all unique permutations of the string s in lexicographically sorted order.

Example
Input:

s = "AAB"

Output:

\["AAB", "ABA", "BAA"]

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ length of s ≤ 8
  • s contains uppercase and lowercase English letters only.

Goal:
Generate all distinct permutations of the string sorted lexicographically without duplicates.

🧠 Approach

  1. Sort the String: Begin with sorting the string to help generate permutations in lexicographical order.
  2. Backtracking with Swaps: Use a recursive approach that swaps characters and generates all possible permutations.
  3. Avoid Duplicates: Use a TreeSet to automatically store permutations in sorted order and avoid duplicates.
  4. Store and Return: Convert the set to a list and return the result.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Sort string characters
  • Initialize an empty TreeSet
  • Call recursive permutation function with index 0
  • For each recursion, swap characters and recurse for next index
  • Add complete permutation to set when base case reached
  • Return sorted list from set
  • End

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function findPermutation(s):
sort s
initialize TreeSet res
permute(0, s as StringBuilder, res)
return list(res)

function permute(index, s, res):
if index == s.length:
res.add(s.toString())
return

for i from index to s.length - 1:
    swap s[index] and s[i]
    permute(index + 1, s, res)
    swap s[index] and s[i] (backtrack)

💻 Java Code

import java.util.*;

class GfG {

    // Recursive function to generate all unique permutations
    static void recurPermute(int index, StringBuilder s, Set<String> ans) {
        // Base Case
        if (index == s.length()) {
            ans.add(s.toString());
            return;
        }

        // Try all swaps and backtrack
        for (int i = index; i < s.length(); i++) {
            // Swap characters at index and i
            char temp = s.charAt(index);
            s.setCharAt(index, s.charAt(i));
            s.setCharAt(i, temp);

            // Recurse
            recurPermute(index + 1, s, ans);

            // Backtrack (restore original string)
            temp = s.charAt(index);
            s.setCharAt(index, s.charAt(i));
            s.setCharAt(i, temp);
        }
    }

    // Main function to find permutations
    static List<String> findPermutation(String s) {
        // Sort the characters to start with lexicographically smallest
        char[] sorted = s.toCharArray();
        Arrays.sort(sorted);
        s = new String(sorted);

        Set<String> res = new TreeSet<>();
        recurPermute(0, new StringBuilder(s), res);

        return new ArrayList<>(res);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s = "ABC";
        List<String> res = findPermutation(s);
        for (String x : res) {
            System.out.print(x + " ");
        }
    }
}

Time Complexity:
O(n * n!), where n is length of the string.

Space Complexity:
O(n!) due to storage of all unique permutations.

Notes:

  • Sorting ensures generation of lex order permutations.
  • Using TreeSet avoids duplicates but incurs log-factor overhead.
  • Backtracking swaps reduce extra space usage compared to building new strings.
  • Edge cases: all identical characters, mixed cases handled correctly.

Problem Statement: 268¶

Shuffle a Given Array using Fisher–Yates Shuffle Algorithm

Given an array, write a program to generate a random permutation of array elements. This is also referred to as:

  • "Shuffle a deck of cards"
  • "Randomize a given array"

The requirement is that every permutation should be equally likely.

🧠 Naive Approach

  1. Create an auxiliary array temp[] and copy arr[] into it.
  2. For each index i in arr[], randomly select an element from temp[], assign it to arr[i], and remove it from temp[].
  3. Time complexity: O(n²).

⚡ Efficient Approach - Fisher–Yates Shuffle The Fisher–Yates shuffle algorithm provides an efficient way to randomize an array in O(n) time.

Idea:

  • Start from the last element and swap it with a randomly selected element from index 0 to current index.
  • Continue reducing the size of the array considered until reaching the first element.

Example
Input:

arr = \[1, 2, 3, 4]

Output:
A random permutation of [1, 2, 3, 4] such as [3, 1, 4, 2].

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ length of array ≤ 10^5
  • Array elements can be any integers.

Goal:
Generate a uniformly random permutation of the array in-place with O(n) time complexity.

Approach:

  • Iterate from the last element to the second element.
  • For each element at index i, pick a random index j such that 0 ≤ j ≤ i.
  • Swap elements at indices i and j.
  • This ensures every permutation has equal probability.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • For i = n-1 down to 1
    • Pick random j in [0, i]
    • Swap arr[i] and arr[j]
  • End

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function shuffle(arr):
for i from arr.length-1 down to 1:
j = random integer from 0 to i
swap arr\[i], arr\[j]

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.Random;
import java.util.Arrays;

public class ShuffleRand {

    // Function to shuffle the array using Fisher–Yates algorithm
    static void randomize(int arr[], int n) {
        Random r = new Random();

        for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) {
            // Pick a random index from 0 to i
            int j = r.nextInt(i + 1);

            // Swap arr[i] with the randomly picked element
            int temp = arr[i];
            arr[i] = arr[j];
            arr[j] = temp;
        }

        // Print the shuffled array
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr));
    }

    // Driver function
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] arr = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8};
        int n = arr.length;
        randomize(arr, n);
    }
}

Time Complexity:
O(n), each element is swapped once.

Space Complexity:
O(1), in-place algorithm.

Notes:

  • The algorithm avoids bias by ensuring uniform selection at each step.
  • Using a proper random number generator is crucial.
  • Naive approaches with extra arrays or repeated random selection may lead to non-uniform distributions or higher complexity.

Problem Statement: 269¶

Program to Check Strength of Password

A password is said to be strong if it satisfies all of the following criteria:

  1. Contains at least one lowercase English character.
  2. Contains at least one uppercase English character.
  3. Contains at least one special character (!@#$%^&*()-+)
  4. Has a minimum length of 8 characters.
  5. Contains at least one digit.

Based on the criteria:

  • A Strong password satisfies all five conditions.
  • A Moderate password satisfies the first three conditions and has a minimum length of 6.
  • Otherwise, the password is Weak.

✅ Input A single string input representing the password.

🔁 Output Print the strength of the password as:

  • Strong
  • Moderate
  • Weak

Example
Input:

"GeeksforGeeks!@12"

Output:

Strong

Constraints:

  • Password length can vary.
  • Characters can be any printable ASCII.

Goal:
Categorize the password into Strong, Moderate, or Weak as per the given criteria.

💡 Approach

  • Use boolean flags for each character type.
  • Iterate over the password string once.
  • Check length and flags to determine strength.

  1. Initialize Flags: Create boolean flags to track the presence of:

    • Lowercase letters
    • Uppercase letters
    • Digits
    • Special characters (from the set !@#$%^&*()-+)

  2. Iterate Through the Password:

    • Loop through each character of the input string.
    • Use Java utility methods like Character.isLowerCase, Character.isUpperCase, and Character.isDigit to update flags accordingly.
    • For special characters, use a predefined HashSet to check membership.

  3. Determine Strength:

    • If all four flags are true and length ≥ 8 → Strong
    • Else if at least one of lowercase, uppercase, or special character is present and length ≥ 6 → Moderate
    • Otherwise → Weak

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Initialize flags
  • For each character in password: update flags
  • Check conditions for Strong, Moderate, Weak
  • Output result

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function checkPasswordStrength(password):
initialize hasLower, hasUpper, hasDigit, hasSpecial to false
for each char in password:
update flags based on char type
if hasLower and hasUpper and hasDigit and hasSpecial and length >= 8:
return "Strong"
else if (hasLower or hasUpper or hasSpecial) and length >= 6:
return "Moderate"
else:
return "Weak"

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class GFG {

    public static void printStrongNess(String input) {
        int n = input.length();
        boolean hasLower = false, hasUpper = false, hasDigit = false, specialChar = false;

        Set<Character> set = new HashSet<Character>(
            Arrays.asList('!', '@', '#', '$', '%', '^', '&', '*', '(', ')', '-', '+')
        );

        for (char i : input.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isLowerCase(i))
                hasLower = true;
            if (Character.isUpperCase(i))
                hasUpper = true;
            if (Character.isDigit(i))
                hasDigit = true;
            if (set.contains(i))
                specialChar = true;
        }

        // Strength of password
        System.out.print("Strength of password:- ");
        if (hasDigit && hasLower && hasUpper && specialChar && (n >= 8))
            System.out.print(" Strong");
        else if ((hasLower || hasUpper || specialChar) && (n >= 6))
            System.out.print(" Moderate");
        else
            System.out.print(" Weak");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String input = "GeeksforGeeks!@12";
        printStrongNess(input);
    }
}

Time Complexity:
O(n), where n is length of the password.

Space Complexity:
O(1), only fixed number of flags and set for special characters.

Notes:

  • Special characters are explicitly defined as !@#$%^&*()-+.
  • The moderate condition requires at least one of lowercase, uppercase, or special character (not digit).
  • Output format includes a prefix "Strength of password:- " before printing the category.

Problem Statement: 270¶

Word Ladder – Shortest Chain to Reach Target Word

Given:

  • An array of strings arr[], where each word has the same length.
  • Two distinct strings: start and target.

Your task is to find the length of the smallest transformation chain from start to target, such that:

  • Only one character can be changed at a time.
  • Every transformed word must exist in the array arr[].

If it is not possible, print 0.

✅ Input

  • A string start – the initial word.
  • A string target – the goal word.
  • A string array arr[] – containing valid words.

🔁 Output

  • An integer representing the minimum number of steps to reach from start to target, where only one letter changes at each step and all intermediate words must exist in arr[].
  • Output 0 if transformation is not possible.

Example
Input:

start = "toon"
target = "plea"
arr = \["poon", "plee", "same", "poie", "plie", "poin", "plea"]

Output:

7

Constraints:

  • All words are of the same length.
  • start and target are distinct strings.
  • Dictionary size can vary.

Goal:
Return minimum number of transformations to convert start to target using dictionary words; return 0 if not possible.

💡 Approach This problem is a classic graph traversal problem and is efficiently solved using Breadth-First Search (BFS).

  • Model words as graph nodes connected if differing by one character.
  • Use BFS from start to find shortest path to target.
  • Track visited words to avoid cycles.

  1. Model as Graph:

    • Treat each word as a node.
    • Connect two nodes if they differ by exactly one character.

  2. Use BFS:

    • Initialize a queue and start BFS from the start word.
    • At each level of BFS, generate all possible one-letter transformations of the current word.
    • If a transformation exists in the dictionary and hasn't been visited, enqueue it.
    • If the target word is found during traversal, return the current depth of BFS.

  3. Edge Cases:

    • If the target is never reached, return 0.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start with start word in queue
  • While queue not empty:
    • For each word at current level:
      • Generate all one-letter transformations
      • If transformation equals target → return level count
      • If valid and unvisited → enqueue
  • Return 0 if target not found

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function wordLadder(start, target, arr):
dictionary = set(arr)
queue = empty queue
enqueue start
steps = 0

while queue not empty:
    steps += 1
    for each word in current queue size:
        current = dequeue
        for each position in word:
            for c in 'a' to 'z':
                newWord = replace char at position with c
                if newWord not in dictionary:
                    continue
                if newWord == target:
                    return steps + 1
                remove newWord from dictionary
                enqueue newWord
return 0

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class GfG {
    static int wordLadder(String start, String target, String[] arr) {
        Set<String> st = new HashSet<>();
        for (String word : arr)
            st.add(word);

        int res = 0;
        int m = start.length();
        Queue<String> words = new LinkedList<>();
        words.add(start);

        while (!words.isEmpty()) {
            ++res;
            int len = words.size();

            for (int i = 0; i < len; ++i) {
                String word = words.poll();

                for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j) {
                    char[] wordArr = word.toCharArray();
                    char ch = wordArr[j];

                    for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; ++c) {
                        wordArr[j] = c;
                        String newWord = new String(wordArr);

                        if (!st.contains(newWord))
                            continue;

                        if (newWord.equals(target))
                            return res + 1;

                        st.remove(newWord);
                        words.add(newWord);
                    }

                    wordArr[j] = ch;
                }
            }
        }

        return 0;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] arr = new String[]{"poon", "plee", "same", "poie", "plie", "poin", "plea"};
        String start = "toon";
        String target = "plea";
        System.out.println(wordLadder(start, target, arr));
    }
}

Time Complexity:
O(N * M * 26), where N is number of words in dictionary, M is length of each word.

Space Complexity:
O(N) for storing dictionary and BFS queue.

Notes:

  • Removing words from dictionary when visited avoids revisiting.
  • BFS guarantees shortest transformation path.
  • If no valid path exists, return 0.

Problem Statement: 271¶

Find the Minimum Number of Moves Needed to Move from One Cell of Matrix to Another

Given a N x N matrix M filled with the following values:

  • 1 represents the Source.
  • 2 represents the Destination.
  • 3 represents an empty cell.
  • 0 represents a wall (blocked cell).

The task is to find the minimum number of moves required to move from the source to the destination while traversing only through blank cells (3). You can move up, down, left, or right in the matrix.

If it is not possible to reach the destination, return 0.

✅ Input

  • A 2D integer array M[][] representing the matrix.

🔁 Output

  • The minimum number of moves required to reach the destination from the source. If it's not possible to reach, output 0.

Example
Input:

M = \[ \[3, 3, 1, 0],
\[3, 0, 3, 3],
\[2, 3, 0, 3],
\[0, 3, 3, 3] ]

Output:

4

Constraints:

  • Matrix size: N x N (typically small, e.g. N ≤ 100)
  • Source and destination exist exactly once
  • Only allowed to move to adjacent blank (3) or destination (2) cells
  • Walls (0) are not passable

Goal:
Return the minimum number of steps to reach from source (1) to destination (2) using only valid cells; return 0 if unreachable.

💡 Approach We can solve this problem using Breadth-First Search (BFS), which is ideal for finding the shortest path in an unweighted grid.

  1. Grid Representation:

    • Each cell in the grid can be considered a node in a graph.
    • We can move to adjacent cells if they are not blocked (0) and are not visited yet.

  2. BFS Traversal:

    • Start BFS from the source (1).
    • For each adjacent unvisited cell (3), mark it as visited and add it to the queue.
    • Continue until the destination (2) is found or all possible paths are exhausted.

  3. Edge Cases:

    • If no valid path exists from source to destination, return 0.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  1. Convert matrix into a graph where each valid cell is a node
  2. Add edges between adjacent valid cells
  3. Use BFS to find the shortest path from source to destination
  4. Track visited nodes to avoid cycles

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function MinimumPath(matrix):
locate source and destination positions
build graph of connected valid positions
initialize queue with source node
set distance of source = 0

while queue not empty:
    current = dequeue
    for each adjacent valid node:
        if not visited:
            mark visited
            update distance
            enqueue

return distance[destination] if reachable else 0

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Queue;

class Graph {
    private int V;
    private ArrayList<ArrayList<Integer>> adj;

    // Constructor
    Graph(int v)
    {
        V = v;
        adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < v; i++)
            adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    }

    // Add edge to graph
    public void AddEdge(int s, int d)
    {
        adj.get(s).add(d);
        adj.get(d).add(s);
    }

    // Level BFS function to find minimum path
    // from source to sink
    public int BFS(int s, int d)
    {
        // Base case
        if (s == d)
            return 0;

        // Make initial distance of all vertex -1
        int[] level = new int[V];
        for (int i = 0; i < V; i++)
            level[i] = -1;

        // Create a queue for BFS
        Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        level[s] = 0;
        queue.add(s);

        while (queue.size() > 0) {
            s = queue.remove();

            // Get all adjacent vertices
            for (int i : adj.get(s)) {
                if (level[i] < 0 || level[i] > level[s] + 1) {
                    level[i] = level[s] + 1;
                    queue.add(i);
                }
            }
        }

        // Return minimum moves from source to sink
        return level[d];
    }
}

class GFG {
    static int N = 4;

    static boolean IsSafe(int i, int j, int[][] M)
    {
        if ((i < 0 || i >= N) || (j < 0 || j >= N) || M[i][j] == 0)
            return false;
        return true;
    }

    // Returns minimum numbers of moves from source (a
    // cell with value 1) to destination (a cell with
    // value 2)
    static int MinimumPath(int[][] M)
    {
        int s = 0, d = 0; // Source and destination
        int V = N * N + 2;
        Graph g = new Graph(V);

        // Create graph with N*N nodes
        int k = 1; // Number of current vertex
        for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
                if (M[i][j] != 0) {
                    // Connect all 4 adjacent cells
                    if (IsSafe(i, j + 1, M))
                        g.AddEdge(k, k + 1);
                    if (IsSafe(i, j - 1, M))
                        g.AddEdge(k, k - 1);
                    if (j < N - 1 && IsSafe(i + 1, j, M))
                        g.AddEdge(k, k + N);
                    if (i > 0 && IsSafe(i - 1, j, M))
                        g.AddEdge(k, k - N);
                }

                // Source index
                if (M[i][j] == 1)
                    s = k;

                // Destination index
                if (M[i][j] == 2)
                    d = k;
                k++;
            }
        }

        // Find minimum moves
        return g.BFS(s, d);
    }

    // Driver program to check the above function
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        int[][] M = { { 3, 3, 1, 0 },
                    { 3, 0, 3, 3 },
                    { 2, 3, 0, 3 },
                    { 0, 3, 3, 3 } };

        int ans = MinimumPath(M);
        System.out.println(ans);
    }
}

Time Complexity:
O(N²) — where N is matrix dimension, due to checking each cell and its 4 neighbors.

Space Complexity:
O(N²) — for graph representation and visited tracking.

Notes:

  • Graph-based BFS ensures shortest path discovery in unweighted grid
  • Coordinate-to-node mapping is done via a 1D index formula: i * N + j + 1
  • Ensure all adjacent indices are within bounds and not walls

Problem Statement: 272¶

Number of Cells a Queen Can Move with Obstacles on the Chessboard

Given a N x N chessboard with a Queen at position (x, y) and K obstacles, the task is to find the number of cells the Queen can move to. The Queen can move in any of the eight directions: up, down, left, right, and diagonals. However, the Queen cannot pass through or move over obstacles.

  • The Queen can move in the following directions:
    • Horizontally: left and right.
    • Vertically: up and down.
    • Diagonally: four diagonal directions.

The Queen stops moving in a given direction if it encounters the edge of the chessboard or an obstacle.

✅ Input

  • n: Size of the chessboard (an n x n grid).
  • k: The number of obstacles on the board.
  • x, y: The position of the Queen.
  • Two arrays, obstPosx[] and obstPosy[], representing the positions of obstacles.

🔁 Output

  • The number of cells that the Queen can move to, excluding the cells with obstacles.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= n <= 10^5 — Size of the chessboard.
  • 0 <= k <= 10^5 — Number of obstacles.
  • 1 <= x, y <= n — Queen's position must lie within the board.
  • 1 <= obstPosx[i], obstPosy[i] <= n — Obstacles are placed within the board boundaries.
  • No duplicate obstacle positions.

Example
Input:

n = 5
k = 3
Queen = (4, 3)
Obstacles = \[(5, 5), (4, 2), (2, 3)]

Output:

10

Goal:
Determine the number of cells a Queen can move to on an n x n board considering the presence of k obstacles.

💡 Approach To solve the problem, we need to consider the following:

  1. Representation of the chessboard: The chessboard has obstacles, and the Queen can move in different directions (horizontally, vertically, diagonally).

  2. Direction Handling: For each direction, we check how far the Queen can move until it either reaches the boundary of the board or encounters an obstacle.

  3. Obstacles: Use a HashMap to store the positions of obstacles, making it easier to check if a move is blocked.

  4. Movement Simulation: For each of the eight directions, simulate the Queen's movement and count how many cells it can move to before it encounters an obstacle or the edge of the board.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

Start
│
▼
Read input (n, k, Queen position, obstacles)
│
▼
Store obstacles in a HashSet
│
▼
For each of the 8 directions:
Move step by step until edge or obstacle
Count valid positions
│
▼
Output total count
│
▼
End

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

1. Initialize directions = \[8 directions as (dx, dy)]
2. Store all obstacle positions in a set as "x-y"
3. Initialize count = 0
4. For each (dx, dy) in directions:
   i = Queen\_x + dx
   j = Queen\_y + dy
   While 1 <= i <= n and 1 <= j <= n and (i-j not in obstacles):
   increment count
   i += dx
   j += dy
5. Return count

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class GFG { 
    static class pair { 
        int first, second; 
        public pair(int first, int second) { 
            this.first = first; 
            this.second = second; 
        }     
    } 
    
    // Return if position is valid on chessboard 
    static boolean range(int n, int x, int y) { 
        return (x <= n && x > 0 && y <= n && y > 0); 
    } 

    // Return the number of moves with a given direction 
    static int check(int n, int x, int y, int xx, int yy, 
                HashMap <pair, Integer> mp) { 
        int ans = 0; 

        // Checking valid move of Queen in a direction. 
        while (range(n, x, y) && !mp.containsKey(new pair(x, y))) { 
            x += xx; 
            y += yy; 
            ans++; 
        } 

        return ans; 
    } 

    // Return the number of position a Queen can move. 
    static int numberofPosition(int n, int k, int x, int y, 
                                int obstPosx[], int obstPosy[]) { 
        int x1, y1, ans = 0; 
        HashMap <pair, Integer> mp = new HashMap<>(); 

        // Mapping each obstacle's position 
        while(k > 0) { 
            k--; 
            x1 = obstPosx[k]; 
            y1 = obstPosy[k]; 

            mp.put(new pair(x1, y1), 1); 
        } 

        // Fetching number of position a queen can 
        // move in each direction. 
        ans += check(n, x + 1, y, 1, 0, mp); 
        ans += check(n, x - 1, y, -1, 0, mp); 
        ans += check(n, x, y + 1, 0, 1, mp); 
        ans += check(n, x, y - 1, 0, -1, mp); 
        ans += check(n, x + 1, y + 1, 1, 1, mp); 
        ans += check(n, x + 1, y - 1, 1, -1, mp); 
        ans += check(n, x - 1, y + 1, -1, 1, mp); 

        return ans; 
    } 

    // Driver program 
    public static void main(String[] args) { 
        int n = 8; // Chessboard size 
        int k = 1; // Number of obstacles 
        int Qposx = 4; // Queen x position 
        int Qposy = 4; // Queen y position 
        int obstPosx[] = { 3 }; // x position of obstacles 
        int obstPosy[] = { 5 }; // y position of obstacles 

        System.out.print(numberofPosition(n, k, Qposx, Qposy, 
                                        obstPosx, obstPosy) + "\n"); 
    } 
}

Time Complexity:

  • O(k + 8*n) in worst case (k for storing obstacles, up to n steps in 8 directions)

Space Complexity:

  • O(k) for obstacle storage

Notes:

  • The diagonal (x-1, y-1) direction is missing in the original code — it must be added for correctness.
  • Use Set<String> like "x-y" instead of custom object to simplify hashing and equality checking.

Problem Statement: 273¶

Number of Paths Given a grid of size m x n, the task is to determine the number of distinct paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. At each step, one can either move down or right. Given the integers m and n, return the number of unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.

  • Note: The test cases are designed such that the answer will always fit within a 32-bit integer.

✅ Input

  • Two integers, m and n, where:
    • m is the number of rows in the grid.
    • n is the number of columns in the grid.

🔁 Output

  • Return the number of unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= m, n <= 100
  • The result will always fit in a 32-bit signed integer.

Example
Input:

m = 3
n = 7

Output:

28

Goal:
Find the total number of distinct right or down paths from the top-left corner (0, 0) to the bottom-right corner (m-1, n-1).

💡 Approach This problem can be solved using Dynamic Programming (DP).

  • We can consider a DP table dp[][] where dp[i][j] represents the number of distinct paths to reach cell (i, j).
  • The base case is that the number of ways to reach any cell in the first row or first column is 1, because there is only one way to reach those cells — by moving straight across the row or column.
  • For other cells, the number of ways to reach them is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above and the cell to the left (i.e., dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]).

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:


Start
│
▼
Initialize 1D dp\[] array with dp\[0] = 1
│
▼
Loop through each row
└─ For each column from 1 to n-1:
└─ dp\[j] += dp\[j - 1]
│
▼
Return dp\[n - 1]
│
▼
End

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

1. Initialize dp\[n] with dp\[0] = 1
2. For i from 0 to m - 1:
   For j from 1 to n - 1:
   dp\[j] = dp\[j] + dp\[j - 1]
3. Return dp\[n - 1]

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    public int numberOfPaths(int m, int n) {
// another method
  //   int path = 1;
        // for (int i = n; i < (m + n - 1); i++) {
        //     path *= i;
        //     path /= (i - n + 1);
        // }
        // return path;

        // Initialize a 1D DP array to store the number of paths
        int[] dp = new int[n];
        dp[0] = 1;  // There's only 1 way to reach the first column

        // Iterate over each row
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            // Update the DP array for each column
            for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) {
                dp[j] += dp[j - 1];  // Number of ways to reach dp[j] is the sum of ways to reach left and above
            }
        }

        return dp[n - 1];  // The answer will be at the bottom-right corner
    }
}

Time Complexity:

  • O(m * n)

Space Complexity:

  • O(n)

Notes:

  • An alternate approach is to use combinatorics:
    C(m + n - 2, m - 1) or C(m + n - 2, n - 1)
    This computes the number of unique permutations of moves.

Problem Statement: 274¶

Permutations of a String Given a string s, which may contain duplicate characters, your task is to generate and return an array of all unique permutations of the string. You can return your answer in any order.

✅ Input

  • A string s of length n where 1 <= n <= 9.

🔁 Output

  • Return an array of strings, where each string is a unique permutation of the input string.

Example Input: s = "aab"

Output: ["aab", "aba", "baa"]

Constraints:

  • 1 <= s.length <= 9
  • s consists of lowercase English letters.

Goal: Generate all unique permutations of the given string, even if it contains duplicate characters.

💡 Approach To generate all unique permutations of a string, we can use backtracking. The idea is to recursively build permutations and ensure that we do not generate duplicate permutations when the string contains repeated characters.

  1. Backtracking:

    • At each step, we pick a character and recursively generate permutations for the remaining characters.
    • To avoid duplicate permutations, we keep track of the count of each character and only use a character if it has not been used up.

  2. Use a HashMap:

    • The HashMap stores the count of each character in the string. This helps to ensure that we generate permutations considering repeated characters.

  3. Recursive Backtracking:

    • The recursion function appends a character to the current permutation, updates its count in the HashMap, and recursively generates the next character.
    • If the current permutation reaches the length of the string, it's added to the result list.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram: (Not provided in original — suggest sketching a recursive decision tree with branching at each character choice, showing backtracking when character counts hit 0.)

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Create a frequency map of characters in the input string.
  2. Define a recursive backtracking function:
    • If current string length == input length, add to result.
    • Loop through each character in map:
      • If count > 0:
        • Append character to current string.
        • Decrease count.
        • Recurse.
        • Backtrack: remove character and restore count.
  3. Return the list of collected permutations.

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    // Helper function to generate permutations
    static void genPermutations(int n, StringBuilder curr, 
                          Map<Character, Integer> cnt, List<String> res) {
      
        // Base case: If the length of current permutation is equal to the length of the string
        if (curr.length() == n) {
            res.add(curr.toString());  // Add the current permutation to the result
            return;
        }

        // Iterate over the characters in the map
        for (Map.Entry<Character, Integer> entry : cnt.entrySet()) {
            char c = entry.getKey();
            int count = entry.getValue();

            // If the character is used up, skip it
            if (count == 0) 
                continue;

            // Include the character in the current permutation
            curr.append(c);

            // Decrease the count of the character
            cnt.put(c, count - 1);

            // Recurse to generate the next character
            genPermutations(n, curr, cnt, res);

            // Backtrack: Remove the character from the current permutation
            curr.deleteCharAt(curr.length() - 1);

            // Restore the count of the character
            cnt.put(c, count);
        }
    }

    // Function to find all unique permutations
    public ArrayList<String> findPermutation(String s) {
        ArrayList<String> res = new ArrayList<>();  // To store the result
        
        // Create a map to count the frequency of each character
        Map<Character, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
        
        // Count the frequency of each character in the string
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) 
            cnt.put(c, cnt.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);

        // Use a StringBuilder to build permutations and backtrack
        StringBuilder curr = new StringBuilder();
        
        // Start generating permutations
        genPermutations(s.length(), curr, cnt, res);
        
        // Return the result containing all unique permutations
        return res;
    }
}

Time Complexity: O(n! * n), where n is the length of the string. This accounts for generating all permutations and copying strings of length n.

Space Complexity: O(n * n!) for storing results and recursion stack (in worst-case unique character scenario).

Notes:

  • Duplicate characters in input are handled by counting frequencies and only using characters with positive count.
  • Order of output doesn't matter as long as all permutations are unique.

Problem Statement: 275¶

Look and Say Pattern Given an integer n, return the nth row of the following look-and-say pattern. The sequence starts as: 1 11 21 1211 111221

Look-and-Say Pattern: To generate a member of the sequence from the previous member, read off the digits of the previous member, counting the number of digits in groups of the same digit. For example:

  • 1 is read off as "one 1" → 11
  • 11 is read off as "two 1s" → 21
  • 21 is read off as "one 2, then one 1" → 1211
  • 1211 is read off as "one 1, one 2, then two 1s" → 111221
  • 111221 is read off as "three 1s, two 2s, then one 1" → 312211

✅ Input

  • A positive integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 30), representing the row number in the look-and-say sequence.

🔁 Output

  • A string representing the nth row of the sequence.

Example Input: n = 5

Output: "111221"

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 30

Goal: Generate the nth term in the look-and-say sequence based on the transformation rule applied to the previous term.

💡 Approach

  1. Base Case: The first row of the sequence is always 1.
  2. Building the Sequence:
    • Starting from the second row, read the digits of the previous row.
    • Count consecutive digits and form the next row based on the count and the digit.
  3. Iterative Construction:
    • Use a list to store the sequence from row 1 to row n.
    • For each row, examine the previous row and construct the current row based on the counting pattern.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start → Initialize first term as "1"
  • Loop from 2 to n:
    • Read digits of previous term
    • Count consecutive digits
    • Form new term using count + digit
  • Output nth term → End

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Initialize sequence[0] = "1"
  2. For i = 1 to n - 1:
    • Set prev = sequence[i - 1]
    • Initialize empty string curr
    • For each digit in prev:
      • Count occurrences of same digit
      • Append count and digit to curr
    • Set sequence[i] = curr
  3. Return sequence[n - 1]

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    // Function to generate the nth row of the Look-and-Say sequence
    static String lookandsay(int n) {
        // List to store the sequence up to the nth row
        List<String> dp = new ArrayList<>(n + 1);
        
        // Base case: The first row is always "1"
        dp.add("1");
        
        // Iterate to generate each row from 2 to n
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
            String prev = dp.get(i - 1 - 1);  // Get the previous row
            String curr = "";  // String to store the current row
            
            // Loop through the previous row to count groups of digits
            for (int j = 0; j < prev.length(); j++) {
                int count = 1;  // Initialize count for the current digit
                // Count consecutive digits
                while (j + 1 < prev.length() && prev.charAt(j) == prev.charAt(j + 1)) {
                    count++;
                    j++;
                }
                // Append the count followed by the digit to the current row
                curr += Integer.toString(count) + prev.charAt(j);
            }
            // Add the current row to the list
            dp.add(curr);
        }
        
        // Return the nth row of the sequence
        return dp.get(n - 1);
    }
}

🚀 Time Complexity Time Complexity: The time complexity of this solution is O(n * m) where n is the row number and m is the length of the string for each row.

Space Complexity: The space complexity is O(n * m) due to the storage of each row in the list.

Notes:

  • This problem emphasizes understanding and implementing string parsing and transformation logic.
  • Strings may grow quickly in size, but constraints ensure performance is manageable.

Problem Statement: 276¶

3 Sum Closest

Given an array arr[] and an integer target, the task is to find the sum of three integers in arr[] such that the sum is closest to target.

Note:

  • If multiple sums are closest to the target, return the maximum one.

✅ Input

  • An integer n representing the size of the array arr[] (3 ≤ n ≤ 1000).
  • An array of integers arr[] (1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 1000).
  • An integer target (-10^4 ≤ target ≤ 10^4).

🔁 Output

  • An integer representing the sum of three integers in the array arr[] that is closest to the target.

Example Input: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], target = 10

Output: 10

Constraints:

  • 3 ≤ n ≤ 1000
  • 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 1000
  • -10^4 ≤ target ≤ 10^4

Goal:
Find the sum of any three integers from the array such that it is closest to the given target. If multiple sums are equally close, return the maximum among them.

💡 Approach

  1. Sorting: First, sort the input array to enable two-pointer technique.
  2. Two-Pointer Technique: For each element, use two pointers (left and right) to find the sum of the current element and two other elements such that their sum is closest to the target.
  3. Tracking Closest Sum: Keep track of the minimum difference between the current sum and the target. If the difference is smaller than the previous minimum, update the result. If the difference is equal, update the result with the maximum sum.
  4. Optimizing: If the current sum is greater than the target, decrease the right pointer. If the sum is smaller, increase the left pointer.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start → Sort array
  • Loop through elements (i = 0 to n-3)
    • Set left = i+1, right = n-1
    • While left < right:
      • Compute currSum = arr[i] + arr[left] + arr[right]
      • If closer than previous → update minDiff and result
      • If equally close and larger → update result
      • Move pointers based on comparison with target
  • End loop → return result

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Sort the array
  2. Initialize res and minDiff
  3. Loop through array:
    • Set left and right pointers
    • While left < right:
      • Compute currSum
      • If |currSum - target| < minDiff → update res
      • Else if equal and currSum > res → update res
      • Move pointers accordingly
  4. Return res

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.Arrays;

class Solution {
    // Function to find the sum of three integers closest to the target
    static int closest3Sum(int[] arr, int target) {
        int n = arr.length;
        Arrays.sort(arr);  // Sort the array
        int res = 0;  // Store the result
        int minDiff = Integer.MAX_VALUE;  // Initialize the minimum difference with the maximum possible value

        // Loop through the array
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) {
            int l = i + 1, r = n - 1;  // Initialize left and right pointers

            // Iterate using two pointers to find the closest sum
            while (l < r) {
                int currSum = arr[i] + arr[l] + arr[r];  // Calculate the current sum

                // Check if the current sum is closer to the target
                if (Math.abs(currSum - target) < minDiff) {
                    minDiff = Math.abs(currSum - target);  // Update the minimum difference
                    res = currSum;  // Update the result with the closest sum
                }
              
                // If the difference is equal, choose the maximum sum
                else if(Math.abs(currSum - target) == minDiff) {
                    res = Math.max(res, currSum);  // Take the maximum sum if multiple sums are equally close
                }

                // Adjust the pointers based on the current sum
                if (currSum > target) {
                    r--;  // Decrease the right pointer if the current sum is greater than the target
                } else {
                    l++;  // Increase the left pointer if the current sum is smaller than the target
                }
            }
        }

        return res;  // Return the closest sum
    }
}

🚀 Time Complexity Time Complexity:
The time complexity is O(n^2), where n is the number of elements in the array. Sorting the array takes O(n log n), and the two-pointer search takes O(n) for each element.

Space Complexity:
The space complexity is O(1), as we are only using a constant amount of extra space.

Notes:

  • The array must have at least 3 elements to form a valid triplet.
  • Handling equal differences with a tie-breaking condition ensures deterministic output.

Problem Statement: 277¶

Let's Play!!! Let’s play a game! 🕹️
Given a matrix mat[][] of size n x m, your task is to check whether the matrix is Super Similar or not.

To perform this task, follow these rules:

  1. Rotation Rule:

    • For even-indexed rows (starting from 0): Rotate left x times.
    • For odd-indexed rows: Rotate right x times.

  2. Final Check:

    • After performing the above transformations, check whether the final matrix is same as the original matrix.
    • If it is, return 1; otherwise, return 0.

✅ Input

  • n: number of rows in the matrix.
  • m: number of columns in the matrix.
  • mat[][]: a 2D integer matrix.
  • x: number of times each row should be rotated.

🔁 Output

  • Return 1 if the matrix is Super Similar, else return 0.

Example Input: n = 2, m = 4, x = 2
mat = [[1, 2, 3, 4],
[5, 6, 7, 8]]

Output: 1

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n, m ≤ 100
  • 1 ≤ mat[i][j] ≤ 10^3
  • 0 ≤ x ≤ 10^4

Goal:
Determine whether the matrix remains unchanged after performing the specified left/right rotations on its rows.

💡 Approach

  1. Backup the Original Matrix:

    • Make a deep copy of the input matrix to compare after rotations.

  2. Normalize Rotations:

    • Since rotating a row m times results in the same row, only use x % m.

  3. Perform Row-wise Rotations:

    • For even-indexed rows: Perform left rotation using reversal technique.
    • For odd-indexed rows: Perform right rotation by converting it to left rotation (m - x).

  4. Compare Matrices:

    • If the rotated matrix is identical to the original, return 1, else return 0.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

  • Start
  • Copy original matrix
  • Normalize x as x % m
  • For each row:
    • if even → left rotate
    • if odd → right rotate
  • Compare rotated matrix with original
  • If equal → return 1; else → return 0

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

  1. Copy original matrix into original[][]
  2. Compute x = x % m
  3. For each row i from 0 to n-1:
    • If i % 2 == 0, rotate row[i] left by x
    • Else, rotate row[i] right by x
  4. Compare all elements of mat[][] with original[][]
  5. If all elements match → return 1
    Else → return 0

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {

    // Main function to check if matrix is Super Similar
    static int isSuperSimilar(int n, int m, int mat[][], int x) {
        // Create a deep copy of the original matrix
        int[][] original = new int[n][m];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            System.arraycopy(mat[i], 0, original[i], 0, m);

        // Normalize x as rotating m times results in the same row
        x = x % m;

        // Perform the required rotations row by row
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (i % 2 == 0) {
                rotateLeft(mat[i], m, x);
            } else {
                rotateRight(mat[i], m, x);
            }
        }

        // Check if the matrix is same as original
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) {
                if (mat[i][j] != original[i][j])
                    return 0;
            }
        }

        return 1;
    }

    // Function to rotate a row to the left by x positions
    static void rotateLeft(int[] row, int m, int x) {
        reverse(row, 0, x - 1);
        reverse(row, x, m - 1);
        reverse(row, 0, m - 1);
    }

    // Function to rotate a row to the right by x positions
    static void rotateRight(int[] row, int m, int x) {
        rotateLeft(row, m, m - x);
    }

    // Helper function to reverse a portion of an array
    static void reverse(int[] row, int start, int end) {
        while (start < end) {
            int temp = row[start];
            row[start] = row[end];
            row[end] = temp;
            start++;
            end--;
        }
    }
}

🚀 Time Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n * m) — as we are iterating through every element of the matrix.
  • Space Complexity: O(n * m) — for storing a copy of the original matrix.

Notes:

  • Rotating left and right by m or any multiple has no effect, hence normalization with modulo.
  • Reversal-based rotation is efficient and avoids extra space.

Problem Statement: 278¶

Word Break (Using Trie) Given a string A and a dictionary of n words B, determine whether A can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words from B. You need to use Trie Data Structure to solve this problem efficiently.

✅ Input

  • A string A (consisting of lowercase English letters).
  • A list B containing n lowercase English words.

🔁 Output

  • Return 1 if the string A can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.
  • Otherwise, return 0.

Example Input: A = "applepenapple"
B = ["apple", "pen"]

Output: 1

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ |A| ≤ 10^4
  • 1 ≤ |B[i]| ≤ 100
  • 1 ≤ |B| ≤ 10^3
  • All strings consist of lowercase English letters only.

Goal:
Determine if the string A can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words from list B using a Trie for efficient lookup.

💡 Approach

  1. Trie Construction:

    • Create a Trie and insert all words from the dictionary B into it.
    • Each node in the Trie corresponds to a character, and we mark the end of valid words with isEnd = true.

  2. Dynamic Programming:

    • Use a boolean array dp of size n+1, where dp[i] indicates whether the substring A[0...i-1] can be segmented using dictionary words.
    • Initialize dp[0] = true (empty string can be segmented).
    • For every index i, check all possible splits j such that if dp[j] == true and substring A[j...i-1] exists in Trie, then set dp[i] = true.

  3. Final Check:

    • Return 1 if dp[n] is true (entire string can be segmented), otherwise return 0.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
\[Insert all words from B into Trie]
↓
\[Initialize dp\[0] = true]
↓
\[For i = 1 to A.length]
↓
┌──────── For j = 0 to i ─────────┐
│ If dp\[j] is true AND            │
│ A\[j to i-1] is in Trie          │
│ → dp\[i] = true, break loop      │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
↓
\[Check if dp\[n] is true → return 1 else return 0]
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function wordBreak(A, B):
build Trie from words in B
n = length of A
dp = boolean array of size n+1
dp\[0] = true

for i from 1 to n:
    for j from 0 to i:
        if dp[j] and A[j:i] is in Trie:
            dp[i] = true
            break

return 1 if dp[n] else 0

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {

    // Trie node definition
    static class TrieNode {
        TrieNode[] children = new TrieNode[26];
        boolean isEnd;

        TrieNode() {
            isEnd = false;
        }
    }

    static TrieNode root;

    // Insert word into Trie
    static void insert(String word) {
        TrieNode curr = root;
        for (char ch : word.toCharArray()) {
            int idx = ch - 'a';
            if (curr.children[idx] == null)
                curr.children[idx] = new TrieNode();
            curr = curr.children[idx];
        }
        curr.isEnd = true;
    }

    // Search substring A[start...end-1] in Trie
    static boolean search(String word, int start, int end) {
        TrieNode curr = root;
        for (int i = start; i < end; i++) {
            int idx = word.charAt(i) - 'a';
            if (curr.children[idx] == null)
                return false;
            curr = curr.children[idx];
        }
        return curr.isEnd;
    }

    // Main function
    public static int wordBreak(String A, ArrayList<String> B) {
        root = new TrieNode();

        // Insert all dictionary words into Trie
        for (String word : B) {
            insert(word);
        }

        int n = A.length();
        boolean[] dp = new boolean[n + 1];
        dp[0] = true;

        // DP to check valid word breaks
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
                if (dp[j] && search(A, j, i)) {
                    dp[i] = true;
                    break;
                }
            }
        }

        return dp[n] ? 1 : 0;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n²) for DP transitions and O(m * l) for inserting m words of length l into the Trie.
  • Space Complexity: O(n + Trie size), where n is the length of string A.

Notes:

  • Trie improves substring lookups over traditional HashSet.
  • Early break in inner loop improves average case performance.
  • Efficient for large dictionaries or long input strings.

Problem Statement: 279¶

Primes Sum Given an integer N, determine if it can be expressed as the sum of two prime numbers.

✅ Input

  • A single integer N (2 ≤ N ≤ 10⁶)

🔁 Output

  • Return "Yes" if N can be expressed as the sum of two prime numbers.
  • Otherwise, return "No".

Example Input: N = 34

Output: Yes

Constraints:

  • 2 ≤ N ≤ 10^6

Goal:
Determine if the given integer N can be represented as the sum of two prime numbers.

💡 Approach

  1. Check for Prime Numbers:

    • Use a helper function isPrime(int num) to check if a number is prime.
    • A number is prime if it's greater than 1 and has no divisors other than 1 and itself.

  2. Search for Two Primes:

    • Iterate from i = 2 to N/2 and check whether both i and N - i are prime.
    • If such a pair exists, return "Yes".

  3. Return "No":

    • If no such pair is found, return "No".

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
\[Input N]
↓
\[Loop i = 2 to N/2]
↓
┌────────────────────────────┐
│ If isPrime(i) AND          │
│ isPrime(N - i)             │
│ → Return "Yes"             │
└────────────────────────────┘
↓
\[Return "No"]
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function isPrime(num):
if num < 2: return false
if num == 2 or num == 3: return true
if num % 2 == 0 or num % 3 == 0: return false
for i from 5 to sqrt(num) step 6:
if num % i == 0 or num % (i + 2) == 0:
return false
return true

function isSumOfTwo(N):
for i from 2 to N/2:
if isPrime(i) and isPrime(N - i):
return "Yes"
return "No"

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    // Function to check if a number is prime
    static boolean isPrime(int num) {
        if (num < 2) return false;
        if (num == 2 || num == 3) return true;
        if (num % 2 == 0 || num % 3 == 0) return false;

        for (int i = 5; i * i <= num; i += 6) {
            if (num % i == 0 || num % (i + 2) == 0)
                return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    // Function to check if N can be expressed as sum of two primes
    static String isSumOfTwo(int N) {
        for (int i = 2; i <= N / 2; i++) {
            if (isPrime(i) && isPrime(N - i)) {
                return "Yes";
            }
        }
        return "No";
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(√N) for checking prime, loop runs up to N/2 → Overall O(N√N) in worst case.
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Notes:

  • The loop limit of i ≤ N/2 ensures all possible unique prime pairs are checked only once.
  • This approach can be optimized further using a sieve if multiple queries are involved.

Problem Statement: 280¶

Total Count

You are given an array arr[] of positive integers and a threshold value k. For each element in the array, divide it into the minimum number of small integers such that each divided integer is less than or equal to k. Your task is to compute the total number of these integers across all elements of the array.

✅ Input

  • An integer k (1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁴)
  • An array arr[] of size n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵), with elements 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁹

🔁 Output

  • Return a single integer representing the total number of resulting integers after dividing all elements based on the given condition.

Example Input: k = 3
arr = [5, 8, 2]

Output: 6

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁴
  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵
  • 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁹

Goal:
Calculate the total number of split integers needed so that no part exceeds k.

💡 Approach

  1. Observation:

    • For each element num, we want the minimum number of parts such that each part is ≤ k.
    • This is equivalent to computing ceil(num / k).

  2. Formula:

    • To compute ceil(num / k) efficiently:
      ceil(num / k) = (num + k - 1) / k

  3. Iterate Through Array:

    • For each element in arr, apply the formula and sum up the result.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
\[Input k, arr\[]]
↓
Initialize total = 0
↓
\[For each num in arr\[]]
↓
Compute parts = (num + k - 1) / k
↓
Add parts to total
↓
\[Return total]
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function totalCount(k, arr):
total = 0
for num in arr:
total += (num + k - 1) / k
return total

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    int totalCount(int k, int[] arr) {
        int total = 0;
        for (int num : arr) {
            total += (num + k - 1) / k;  // Equivalent to ceil(num / k)
        }
        return total;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the size of the array.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), only a running sum is stored.

Notes:

  • (num + k - 1) / k ensures we always round up the division without using floating-point operations.
  • This method is efficient even for very large arrays and values.

Problem Statement: 281¶

K-Pangrams

Given a string str and an integer k, return true if the string can be changed into a pangram after at most k operations, else return false.

🔁 Definition:

  • A pangram is a sentence that contains every letter in the English alphabet at least once.
  • One operation consists of swapping an existing alphabetic character with any other lowercase alphabetic character.

✅ Input

  • A string str containing lowercase alphabetic characters.
  • An integer k representing the maximum allowed operations.

🔁 Output

  • Return true if the string can be transformed into a pangram in at most k operations, otherwise return false.

Example Input: str = "thequickbrownfxjmpsvlazydg", k = 1

Output: true

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ str.length ≤ 10⁵
  • 0 ≤ k ≤ 26
  • str contains only lowercase English letters

Goal:
Determine if a given string can be converted to a pangram using at most k letter substitutions.

💡 Approach

  1. Track Unique Letters:

    • Use a boolean array seen[26] to mark which characters have already appeared.

  2. Count Total Alphabetic Characters:

    • Keep track of totalAlpha, the count of lowercase alphabetic characters.

  3. Compute Missing Characters:

    • A pangram requires all 26 letters.
    • If fewer than 26 letters are present in the string, it's impossible to transform into a pangram.

  4. Decision Based on Operations:

    • Calculate how many unique letters are missing: missing = 26 - unique.
    • Return true if missing <= k.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Input: str, k
↓
Initialize seen\[26], unique = 0, totalAlpha = 0
↓
For each char c in str:
if c is between 'a' and 'z':
totalAlpha++
if not seen\[c - 'a']:
seen\[c - 'a'] = true
unique++
↓
If totalAlpha < 26 → return false
↓
missing = 26 - unique
↓
If missing ≤ k → return true
Else → return false
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function kPangram(str, k):
seen = array\[26] of false
unique = 0
totalAlpha = 0

for char in str:
    if is_lowercase_letter(char):
        totalAlpha += 1
        if not seen[char - 'a']:
            seen[char - 'a'] = true
            unique += 1

if totalAlpha < 26:
    return false

missing = 26 - unique
return missing <= k

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    boolean kPangram(String str, int k) {
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[26];
        int unique = 0;
        int totalAlpha = 0;

        for (char c : str.toCharArray()) {
            if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') {
                totalAlpha++;
                int idx = c - 'a';
                if (!seen[idx]) {
                    seen[idx] = true;
                    unique++;
                }
            }
        }

        if (totalAlpha < 26) return false;

        int missing = 26 - unique;
        return missing <= k;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the length of the string.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), fixed-size array of 26 letters.

Notes:

  • It's impossible to form a pangram if the string has fewer than 26 alphabetic characters.
  • Swapping allows replacement of letters, but cannot increase the number of alphabetic characters.

Problem Statement: 282¶

Array Duplicates Given an array arr of integers, find all the elements that occur more than once in the array.
If no element repeats, return an empty array.

✅ Input

  • An array of integers arr[].

🔁 Output

  • A list of integers that appear more than once in the array, sorted in ascending order.
  • Return an empty list if no duplicates exist.

Example
Input:
arr = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]

Output:
[2, 3]

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 10⁵
  • -10⁹ ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁹

Goal:
Return a sorted list of all elements that appear more than once in the array.

💡 Approach

  1. Frequency Count:
    • Use a hash map to store the frequency of each element.
  2. Collect Duplicates:
    • Iterate through the map and collect keys with frequency > 1.
  3. Sort the Result:
    • Sort the list of duplicates before returning.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Input: arr\[]
↓
Initialize HashMap freq
↓
For each num in arr:
freq\[num] += 1
↓
Initialize result list
↓
For each (key, value) in freq:
if value > 1:
add key to result
↓
Sort result
↓
Return result
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function findDuplicates(arr):
freq = empty hashmap
result = empty list

for num in arr:
    if num in freq:
        freq[num] += 1
    else:
        freq[num] = 1

for key, val in freq:
    if val > 1:
        result.add(key)

sort(result)
return result

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    public List<Integer> findDuplicates(int[] arr) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();

        // Count the frequency of each element
        for (int num : arr) {
            freq.put(num, freq.getOrDefault(num, 0) + 1);
        }

        // Find elements that occur more than once
        for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> entry : freq.entrySet()) {
            if (entry.getValue() > 1) {
                res.add(entry.getKey());
            }
        }

        // Sort the result
        Collections.sort(res); 
        return res;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n log n)
    • O(n) for counting frequencies
    • O(n log n) for sorting the results
  • Space Complexity: O(n)
    • For storing frequencies and result list

Notes:

  • Sorting ensures output consistency regardless of input order.
  • Edge case: If all elements are unique, return an empty list.

Problem Statement: 283¶

Find Missing in Second Array

Given two integer arrays a and b, the task is to find the numbers which are present in the first array a, but not present in the second array b.

📝 Note: The result should maintain the order of elements as they appear in array a.

✅ Input

  • Two integer arrays a[] and b[].

🔁 Output

  • A list of integers that are present in a but not in b, maintaining the original order from array a.

Example
Input:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
b = [2, 4, 6]

Output:
[1, 3, 5]

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ a.length, b.length ≤ 10⁵
  • -10⁹ ≤ a[i], b[i] ≤ 10⁹

Goal:
Identify and return elements from array a that are not present in array b, maintaining the order.

💡 Approach

  1. Store Elements of b in a Set:
    • This allows O(1) average lookup time.
  2. Iterate Over a:
    • For each element, check if it exists in the set created from b.
    • If not, add it to the result list.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Input: a\[], b\[]
↓
Initialize setB with elements of b
↓
Initialize result list
↓
For each num in a:
if num not in setB:
add num to result
↓
Return result
↓
\[End]

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function findMissing(a, b):
setB = set(b)
result = empty list

for num in a:
    if num not in setB:
        result.append(num)

return result

💻 Java Implementation

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    ArrayList<Integer> findMissing(int[] a, int[] b) {
        HashSet<Integer> setB = new HashSet<>();
        ArrayList<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();

        // Store elements of b in a set
        for (int num : b) {
            setB.add(num);
        }

        // Check which elements of a are not in b
        for (int num : a) {
            if (!setB.contains(num)) {
                result.add(num);
            }
        }

        return result;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n + m)
    • Where n is the length of array a, and m is the length of array b.
  • Space Complexity: O(m)
    • For storing elements of array b in a set.

Notes:

  • Using a set ensures efficient membership testing.
  • Preserving the input order from array a is important for correctness.

Problem Statement: 284¶

Leap Year You are given an integer N. Return true if it is a Leap Year, otherwise return false.

✅ Input

  • An integer N representing a year.

🔁 Output

  • A boolean true or false indicating whether the year is a leap year.

📘 Definition: Leap Year A year is a leap year if:

  • It is divisible by 4, and
    • Not divisible by 100, unless it is also divisible by 400.

Examples:

  • 2000 → Leap Year (divisible by 400)
  • 1900 → Not a Leap Year (divisible by 100 but not 400)
  • 2012 → Leap Year (divisible by 4 and not by 100)
  • 2019 → Not a Leap Year

Example
Input:
2000
1900
2012
2019

Output:
true
false
true
false

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ N ≤ 10⁹

Goal:
Determine whether a given year N is a leap year based on the leap year rules.

💡 Approach

  1. Check if N is divisible by 4.
  2. If true, check:
    • If N is divisible by 100:
      • Then it must also be divisible by 400 to be a leap year.
    • If N is not divisible by 100, then it's a leap year.
  3. If not divisible by 4, it's not a leap year.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

\[Start]
↓
Input: Year N
↓
Is N % 4 == 0?
↓         ↓
No         Yes
↓           ↓
Return       Is N % 100 == 0?
false         ↓         ↓
No         Yes
↓           ↓
Return       Is N % 400 == 0?
true        ↓       ↓
No        Yes
↓          ↓
Return      Return
false        true

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

function isLeap(N):
if N % 4 != 0:
return false
if N % 100 != 0:
return true
if N % 400 == 0:
return true
return false

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    static boolean isLeap(int N) {
        // Check for leap year conditions
        if (N % 4 == 0) {
            if (N % 100 == 0) {
                return N % 400 == 0;
            } else {
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(1)
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Notes:

  • Leap year logic handles exceptions like century years (e.g., 1900).
  • Constant time check based only on divisibility.

Problem Statement: 285¶

Element with Left Side Smaller and Right Side Greater

Given an unsorted array arr[], find the first element in the array such that all elements on its left are smaller and all elements on its right are greater than it.

📌 Note:
Return -1 if no such element exists.

✅ Input

  • An integer array arr[].

🔁 Output

  • Return the first element that satisfies the condition.
  • If no such element exists, return -1.

Example
Input:
[4, 2, 5, 7]
[11, 9, 12, 15, 13, 16, 17]

Output:
5
12

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^6
  • -10^9 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10^9

Goal:
Find the first element in the array such that all elements on its left are smaller and all elements on its right are greater.

💡 Approach

  1. Left Max Array:
    • Create an array leftMax[] such that leftMax[i] holds the maximum element to the left of index i.
  2. Right Min Array:
    • Create an array rightMin[] such that rightMin[i] holds the minimum element to the right of index i.
  3. Traversal:
    • For each element from index 1 to n-2, check:
      • arr[i] >= leftMax[i] and arr[i] <= rightMin[i]
      • If both conditions are met, return arr[i].

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

Start
↓
Input arr\[]
↓
Create leftMax\[] and rightMin\[]
↓
For i from 1 to n-2:
if arr\[i] >= leftMax\[i-1] and arr\[i] <= rightMin\[i+1]
return arr\[i]
↓
If no element found, return -1

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

leftMax\[0] = arr\[0]
for i in 1 to n-1:
leftMax\[i] = max(leftMax\[i-1], arr\[i])

rightMin\[n-1] = arr\[n-1]
for i in n-2 down to 0:
rightMin\[i] = min(rightMin\[i+1], arr\[i])

for i in 1 to n-2:
if arr\[i] >= leftMax\[i-1] and arr\[i] <= rightMin\[i+1]:
return arr\[i]

return -1

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    public int findElement(int[] arr) {
        int n = arr.length;
        int[] leftMax = new int[n];
        int[] rightMin = new int[n];

        // Fill left max array
        leftMax[0] = arr[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++)
            leftMax[i] = Math.max(leftMax[i - 1], arr[i]);

        // Fill right min array
        rightMin[n - 1] = arr[n - 1];
        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--)
            rightMin[i] = Math.min(rightMin[i + 1], arr[i]);

        // Check for the required element
        for (int i = 1; i < n - 1; i++) {
            if (arr[i] >= leftMax[i] && arr[i] <= rightMin[i]) {
                return arr[i];
            }
        }

        return -1;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n)
  • Space Complexity: O(n) (for leftMax[] and rightMin[])

Notes:

  • The condition uses strict comparisons on neighbors to ensure the element stands out.
  • Edge elements cannot be valid since they lack left or right neighbors fully.

Problem Statement: 286¶

Middle of a Linked List Given the head of a linked list, find the middle node.

  • If the list has odd number of nodes, return the middle one.
  • If the list has an even number of nodes, return the second middle node.

✅ Input

  • The head node of a singly linked list.

🔁 Output

  • Return the data of the middle node as an integer.

Example
Input:
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6
Output:
4

🧠 Example Input:
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5
Output:
3

Constraints:

  • Number of nodes in the linked list: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5
  • Node values can be any integer.

Goal:
Find the middle node of the linked list; if even number of nodes, return the second middle.

💡 Approach Use the Tortoise and Hare Algorithm:

  • Initialize two pointers: slow and fast, both starting at the head.
  • Move slow one step at a time, and fast two steps.
  • When fast reaches the end of the list, slow will be at the middle.

This method ensures that for even-length lists, the second middle is returned.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

Start
↓
Initialize slow and fast at head
↓
While fast != null and fast.next != null:
slow = slow\.next
fast = fast.next.next
↓
Return slow\.data

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

slow = head
fast = head

while fast != null and fast.next != null:
slow = slow\.next
fast = fast.next.next

return slow\.data

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    int getMiddle(Node head) {
        Node slow_ptr = head;
        Node fast_ptr = head;

        while (fast_ptr != null && fast_ptr.next != null) {
            fast_ptr = fast_ptr.next.next;
            slow_ptr = slow_ptr.next;
        }

        return slow_ptr.data;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n)
  • Space Complexity: O(1)

Notes:

  • This approach naturally returns the second middle node when the list length is even.
  • Works in a single pass with constant space.

Problem Statement: 287¶

Roman Number to Integer Given a string in Roman number format (s), your task is to convert it to an integer. Various symbols and their values are given below:

  • I = 1
  • V = 5
  • X = 10
  • L = 50
  • C = 100
  • D = 500
  • M = 1000

✅ Input

  • A string s representing the Roman numeral. The string length will be between 1 and 15.

🔁 Output

  • Return an integer corresponding to the Roman numeral.

🧠 Example Input:
s = "III"
Output:
3

Example
Input:
s = "IX"
Output:
9

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ length of s ≤ 15
  • s contains only valid Roman numerals (I, V, X, L, C, D, M).

Goal:
Convert the Roman numeral string to its integer equivalent.

💡 Approach

  1. Create a map to store Roman numeral characters and their corresponding integer values.
  2. Traverse the Roman numeral string from left to right.
  3. If a numeral is smaller than the next numeral (e.g., I before V), subtract its value from the total. Otherwise, simply add its value.
  4. Return the result after processing the entire string.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

Start
↓
Create map of Roman numerals → integer values
↓
Initialize result = 0
↓
For each character in string s:
If current char value < next char value:
Subtract current from result
Skip next char
Else:
Add current char value to result
↓
Return result

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

map = {'I':1, 'V':5, 'X':10, 'L':50, 'C':100, 'D':500, 'M':1000}
res = 0
i = 0
while i < length of s:
if i+1 < length and map\[s\[i]] < map\[s\[i+1]]:
res += map\[s\[i+1]] - map\[s\[i]]
i += 2
else:
res += map\[s\[i]]
i += 1
return res

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    // Finds decimal value of a given roman numeral
    public int romanToDecimal(String s) {
        HashMap<Character, Integer> romanMap = new HashMap<>();
        romanMap.put('I', 1);
        romanMap.put('V', 5);
        romanMap.put('X', 10);
        romanMap.put('L', 50);
        romanMap.put('C', 100);
        romanMap.put('D', 500);
        romanMap.put('M', 1000);

        int res = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            if (i + 1 < s.length() && romanMap.get(s.charAt(i)) < 
                					romanMap.get(s.charAt(i + 1))) {
                res += romanMap.get(s.charAt(i + 1)) - 
                  					romanMap.get(s.charAt(i));
                i++;
            }
            else {
                res += romanMap.get(s.charAt(i));
            }
        }

        return res;
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the length of the string s.
  • Space Complexity: O(1), since the map size is constant and does not depend on the size of the input.

Notes:

  • Handles subtractive notation like IV (4), IX (9), XL (40), etc.
  • Processes string in a single pass for efficiency.

Problem Statement: 288¶

Run Length Encoding

Given a string s, your task is to complete the function encode that returns the run-length encoded string for the given string. For example, if the input string is "wwwwaaadexxxxxx", the function should return "w4a3d1e1x6". You are required to complete the function encode that takes only one argument, the string which is to be encoded, and returns the encoded string.

✅ Input

  • A string s (1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1000) which may contain only lowercase alphabetic characters.

🔁 Output

  • A string representing the run-length encoding of the input string.

🧠 Example Input:
s = "wwwwaaadexxxxxx"

Output:
"w4a3d1e1x6"

Example
Input:
s = "aabbcc"
Output:
"a2b2c2"

Constraints:

  • 1 ≤ length of s ≤ 1000
  • s contains only lowercase alphabetic characters.

Goal:
Return the run-length encoded string for the input.

💡 Approach

  1. Initialize a counter variable count to 1.
  2. Iterate through the string starting from the second character.
  3. If the current character is the same as the previous one, increment the counter.
  4. If the current character is different from the previous one, append the character and its count to the result.
  5. At the end of the loop, append the last character and its count.
  6. Return the final encoded string.

🧮 Flowchart/ Diagram:

Start
↓
Initialize count = 1, result = ""
↓
For i = 1 to length(s)-1:
If s\[i] == s\[i-1]:
count++
Else:
Append s\[i-1] + count to result
Reset count = 1
↓
Append last character + count to result
↓
Return result

Pseudocode/Algorithm:

count = 1
result = ""
for i in range(1, len(s)):
if s\[i] == s\[i-1]:
count += 1
else:
result += s\[i-1] + str(count)
count = 1
result += s\[-1] + str(count)
return result

💻 Java Implementation

class Solution {
    public static String encode(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.length() == 0) {
            return "";
        }
        
        StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();
        int count = 1;
        
        for (int i = 1; i < s.length(); i++) {
            if (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(i - 1)) {
                count++; 
            } else {
                result.append(s.charAt(i - 1)).append(count);
                count = 1;
            }
        }
        result.append(s.charAt(s.length() - 1)).append(count);
        
        return result.toString();
    }
}

🚀 Time and Space Complexity

  • Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the length of the string s. We are iterating through the string once.
  • Space Complexity: O(n), since we are storing the result string in a StringBuilder.

Notes:

  • Handles consecutive repeating characters by counting their occurrences.
  • Uses a single pass to achieve O(n) time complexity.
  • Uses StringBuilder in Java for efficient string concatenation.

Problem Statement: 289¶

Palindrome String

You are given a string s. Your task is to determine if the string is a palindrome. A string is considered a palindrome if it reads the same forwards and backwards.

✅ Input

  • A string s (1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1000), consisting of lowercase English letters.

🔁 Output

  • Return true if the string is a palindrome, and false otherwise.

🧠 Example Input:
s = "racecar"

Output:
true

Example
Input:
s = "madam"
Output:
true

Constraints:
